qa.q: Does the 2.2-nat recall gap measure induction, or just that bigrams repeated within a window are frequent and easy?
qa.a: Unknown. The measurement does not control for frequency, and repeated bigrams skew toward common ones, so part of the 4.475 vs 6.704 gap is unigram/bigram statistics. Build the controlled metric. Without it, a move in L3 cannot be attributed to L2.
qa.decides: target metric "recall-token loss" vs a frequency-controlled metric (second vs first in-window occurrence of rank>1000 bigrams)

qa.q: Does the baseline form an induction head inside the 1525-step budget anyway?
qa.a: Unknown for this setup. Olsson et al. saw the phase change at roughly 2.5–5B tokens in their models (https://transformer-circuits.pub/2022/in-context-learning-and-induction-heads/index.html). Muon-trained small models learn far faster, so that number does not transfer. Layer-0 entropy of 0.957 at step 100 shows no sharp positional head yet. If the baseline forms one by step ~300, the conv only buys a head start, and the step-1525 gap may shrink below 0.005.
qa.decides: taps in all 12 layers vs only early layers; also whether the end-of-run gain can persist or only the curve shifts earlier

qa.q: Which optimizer group and which parameterisation should the taps get?
qa.a: `build_optimizers` sends every 2-D parameter not named tok/head to Muon. A (4,768) tap tensor would get orthogonalised updates scaled by sqrt(768/4)≈13.9 at lr 0.02, which wrecks it. In AdamW, wd 0.1 at lr 3e-3 pulls a raw identity tap down by about e^-0.38≈0.68 over the run when no gradient opposes it. Use the delta form, route it to AdamW explicitly or store it 3-D, and preferably give it wd 0.
qa.decides: raw kernel with identity tap vs delta form (kv + Σ w_l·shift(kv,l), w init 0); Muon vs AdamW

qa.q: Should the taps go before or after `k_norm`, and do they touch the rotary key?
qa.a: Put them before, on the contiguous `kv = expand(...)` of shape (B,T,768). k_norm then re-normalises the mixed key, so QK-norm still holds logit scale. A conv after k_norm would change key RMS and the effective 1/sqrt(96) temperature. Leave `kr` (shared 32-dim rope key) and `qr` untouched so position encoding stays per-token.
qa.decides: conv on `kv` before view/k_norm vs on k after k_norm

qa.q: Should the taps sit on the 768 expanded channels or on the 128-dim latent?
qa.a: Expanded gives independent kernels for key and value channels, per head, so a head can have prev-token keys and current-token values at once. That is the exact induction wiring. The latent version shares each kernel between every k and v channel that reads that latent dim and relies on `expand` to route. Primer puts its depthwise conv after the per-head projections (https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.08668). Both are far under C3, so pick expanded.
qa.decides: expanded (36,864 params) vs latent before latent_norm (6,144 params)

qa.q: Should it be implemented with `F.conv1d` or with shift-and-add?
qa.a: Shift-add on the contiguous (B,T,768) tensor avoids two transposes and copies, and costs three fused-ish elementwise ops per layer. Cast the taps with `.to(kv.dtype)` like the script does for the mixing weights, otherwise fp32 upcasts double the memory of those tensors. The step-time cost is unmeasured. Belief: 1–3% given that the 4-stream mixing already does similar elementwise work.
qa.decides: conv1d with (B,C,T) transposes vs F.pad shift-add on (B,T,C)

qa.q: Can a recall-only gain pass C7?
qa.a: Overall Δ ≈ 0.13·Δrecall + 0.87·Δrest, so recall tokens alone must improve by ≥0.04 nats just to clear the 0.005 margin. p<0.01 at 3 seeds needs more than that, and seed std is unmeasured. Primer reports MDHA gains in overall LM loss, not only on repeats (https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.08668). L5 therefore depends on phrase-level effects on non-recall tokens too.
qa.decides: kv-only (recall-targeted) vs a broader q/k/v version aimed at all tokens

qa.q: Should the taps also go on queries?
qa.a: Induction needs only shifted keys. Primer convolves Q, K and V with kernel 3 (https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.08668). If q is added, apply it only to the 64 content dims of the 576-wide `wq` output, never to the 32 rope dims. Start with kv-only for clean attribution.
qa.decides: kv-only vs q-content + kv

qa.q: Can the conv leak future tokens into the exam?
qa.a: The shift must be `F.pad(kv, (0,0,l,0))[:, :T]`, i.e. position t reads t−l. A reversed shift leaks x_{t+1}, gives a spuriously low loss, and the harness exam would reward it. The builder must check that changing idx[:, t+1] leaves logits[:, :t+1] unchanged. Positions 0–2 see zero padding in both training and exam windows, so the two are consistent.
qa.decides: left pad (lags 0..3) vs any centred/right pad; whether a causality test is mandatory

qa.q: Does the 45-step/1000-step test plan match the real schedule?
qa.a: `lr_mult` uses `total_steps = smoke_steps`, so a 1000-step smoke run has a different schedule from the 1525-step run (warmup 30, cooldown from 1067). Both arms must use the same steps setting. Recall-loss checkpoints are not logged by the script, so they need a separate probe. KNOWN - `kv = expand(latent_norm(compress(x)))` is (B,T,768) and is viewed as (B,T,6,128) per head, then chunked into k(64) and v(64). A per-channel conv on `kv` before the view is equivalent to per-head k/v convs [script] - q and k are 96 wide (64 content + 32 decoupled rope, one shared rope key head); SDPA default scal
qa.decides: `--smoke-steps 1000` (schedule compressed, cooldown from step 700) vs the full-run schedule truncated at 1000

Newton-Schulz then orthogonalizes a 768x4 matrix, and the shape scale `max(1, 768/4)**0.5 ≈ 13.9` turns lr 0.02 into about 0.28 per step on taps of magnitude abo

nodes.premortem_verdict: The conv shortcuts an induction circuit that the 12-layer baseline builds on its own within the first few hundred steps, and the conv on V blurs exactly the token being copied. Any recall gain on 13% of tokens fades by the end of the cooldown to well under 0.005 nats overall, inside the noise of 3 s

qa.q: Does next-token prediction on recall tokens actually need the copy offset, or is it already implicit in which head did the copying?
qa.a: In the standard induction circuit, the previous-token head always attends at offset 1, so its offset is implied by the head's identity. The induction head's prediction (the token after the earlier match) does not depend on how far back the match was. So the offset is mostly redundant for plain recall, and L4's gain probably comes from variable-offset heads, if it comes at all. This is a belief; it is unmeasured here.
qa.decides: rotate every layer vs only layers whose heads attend at variable offsets (≥ mid-depth)

qa.q: Which frequencies should rotate the value: all 16 of the existing cache (32 dims) or a band?
qa.a: `rope_cache(T, 32, 10000)` gives wavelengths 2π·10000^(k/16) for k = 0..15, from 6.3 up to about 35,300 tokens. - For k ≥ 13, the angle over the whole 1023-token window is under 0.6 rad, so those dims carry almost no offset information. - For k ≤ 2 (wavelengths 6–20), the phase aliases, and these dims cancel hardest under diffuse attention. - k = 3..10 covers wavelengths of about 35–1990 tokens, which is the "32 to 2048" range the first variant actually states. Note that variant's label is wrong: its "longest 8 wavelengths" would be k = 8..15, not 32–2048. I recommend the 16-dim band k = 3..10
qa.decides: 32 dims with `cos, sin` as-is vs 16 dims using `cos[:, 3:11]`, `sin[:, 3:11]`

qa.q: How bad is the content loss from cancellation in the shallow, near-uniform layers?
qa.a: With near-uniform attention over n tokens, |Σ a_ij e^{iωδ}| ≈ |sin(ωn/2)| / (n·sin(ω/2)), which is far below 1 except for the slowest ω. Layer 0 has entropy 0.957, so its rotated slice will carry close to zero content. Its attention gradient norm is already anomalous (0.24 against about 0.02 in its neighbours, z = 7 over 3 seeds), so perturbing layer 0's value path is the riskiest place. That last point is a belief.
qa.decides: apply in all 12 layers vs skip layers 0–2

qa.q: Is the inverse rotation exactly what `apply_rope` can do, and is the pairing right?
qa.a: `apply_rope` pairs dim i with dim i+D/2 inside the tensor it is given, and slices `cos[:T]`. So these calls give the exact inverse at query position i: - `apply_rope(v[..., :32], cos, sin)` for the forward rotation - `apply_rope(y[..., :32], cos, -sin)` for the inverse For the 16-dim band, call it on a 16-dim slice with `cos[:, 3:11]` and `sin[:, 3:11]` (8 pairs). Apply it to `y` while `y` is still (B, H, T, 64), before the transpose. This is read from the script.
qa.decides: reuse `apply_rope(y, cos, -sin)` vs write a new helper

qa.q: Can `wo` (linear) and the MLP actually decode offset from R(ωδ)v_j?
qa.a: The output is bilinear in content and offset. A linear readout recovers the offset only along directions where v_j is consistent across tokens. Values have no bias, and latent RMSNorm does not guarantee such a direction, so decoding depends on the downstream SwiGLU. This is unknown empirically; the build stays faithful (content rotation only), and the carrier version is listed below as a separate idea.
qa.decides: rotate content only (the idea as written) vs also add a constant carrier pair whose rotated output is a pure offset spectrum

qa.q: Is a 45-step kill check long enough to see a recall effect, and is 0.03 nats above seed noise?
qa.a: Unknown. 45 steps is about 1.47M tokens. Much of the 2.2-nat recall advantage at step 100 is likely repeated-bigram frequency rather than induction, and whether induction heads have formed by 1.5M tokens at 21M params is unmeasured. The seed-to-seed spread of recall loss is not in the brief. Measure it on 3 baseline seeds before using 0.03 as a kill threshold.
qa.decides: kill at 45 steps vs extend the check to 100 steps (or a 10M-token mid-run)

qa.q: What do step time and memory cost?
qa.a: The extra work is two elementwise rotations per layer on tensors of (4, 6, 1024, ≤32), which is negligible next to the attention and MLP matmuls. Saved activations add roughly 3 MB per layer at bf16, about 40 MB total, well under the 5.6 GB cap. +1% step time is plausible. Use `torch.cat` rather than in-place writes so autograd stays simple. This is a belief from the arithmetic.
qa.decides: inline slicing and `torch.cat` vs in-place slice assignment to avoid copies

qa.q: Is there prior evidence for rotating values and un-rotating outputs?
qa.a: Not from the brief, and none of its sources tests it. My recollection is that Su Jianlin's blog discussed "VO-RoPE" (rotating V and O) in 2025 without a clear LM gain, but I could not verify a URL, so treat this as unverified.
qa.decides: build as a leap vs deprioritize

qa.q: Does the change survive the harness exam, which builds `GPT(cfg)` from the saved config?
qa.a: No parameters or buffers are added, so `model.pt`'s `state_dict` is unchanged. A new `Config` field is only safe if the exam rebuilds `Config` from this file. Hardcode the constants in `Attention`, as `rd = 32` already is.
qa.decides: new `Config` fields (`v_rope_dims`, band) vs hardcoded constants in `Attention`

qa.q: Should value phases be per-head, given the rotary key is shared across heads?
qa.a: The script uses one cache for all heads, so all heads share the value frequencies, and heads differ only through their attention patterns. Per-head frequencies are a separate idea (STRENGTHEN below), not part of the faithful build. This is from the script.
qa.decides: one shared cos/sin for all heads vs per-head frequency offsets

nodes.cluster_name: Gated nonlinear KV path (latent or expansion)

qa.q: Is the 128-dim latent a real bottleneck here, or would the same 49k params per layer do more as a wider linear latent?
qa.a: Unknown. The only small-scale evidence says a half-rank latent costs about 0.3% loss vs MHA (https://arxiv.org/html/2506.09342v2). Here the latent is a third of d, so the bottleneck is plausible but unproven. The builder should run the equal-param wider latent as the control arm. Without it, a win cannot be credited to nonlinearity.
qa.decides: gated 128-dim latent vs ungated latent widened to about 170 (42 × (384+768) = 48.4k params per layer, equal budget)

qa.q: silu gate at default std-0.02 init, or 2·sigmoid gate with zero-initialised `W_g` (identical to the current model at step 0)?
qa.a: The input x is the RMS-normed read with RMS about 1. `W_g x` therefore has std about 0.02·√384 ≈ 0.39, where silu(z) ≈ z/2 + z²/4. At init the latent is roughly the product of two independent random projections. The linear code the current model starts from is gone, and the latent's sign depends on `W_g x`. RMSNorm cancels the overall 0.5 scale but not this. A zero-init 2·sigmoid gate starts as the current model exactly, because a uniform gate is erased by the latent norm, and then learns relative selection. The spec says silu ("do not water it down"), so build silu. L3 (step-26 loss) is the c
qa.decides: `silu(W_g x)` with `_init` std 0.02 vs `2*sigmoid(W_g x)` with `W_g` zeroed

qa.q: Which variant: gate on the input before the norm (the idea), or gated expansion `expand(c)*silu(gate(c))` (the alternative)?
qa.a: Choose the input gate. Its output passes through `latent_norm`, so V's scale stays at about 0.02·√128 ≈ 0.23 as now. The expansion gate multiplies V, which is not normed, by silu of a std-0.23 signal (≈ 0.12). That shrinks V and the attention output about 8x at init, on top of the already small `wo` init. The expansion gate also costs twice the params (98k per layer).
qa.decides: 384→128 gate before `latent_norm` vs 128→768 gate after it

qa.q: Can a 45-step smoke run resolve a 0.01-nat difference?
qa.a: Probably not. At step 45 (about 1.5M tokens) the loss is around 6.6 and falling fast. Layer-0 attention entropy is 0.957 (near flat) even at step 100, so attention carries little of the loss that early. Seed-to-seed spread at step 45 is unmeasured. The kill should use the step-100 recall-token loss and overall loss across seeds. The step-45 run stays as a crash and VRAM check.
qa.decides: kill on mean loss over steps 40–45 vs kill on matched-step loss at step 100–150 over 2–3 seeds

qa.q: Should the target metric be rare-token loss or recall-token loss?
qa.a: Use recall tokens. The K/V being changed belong to context tokens, and they affect a target only through attention. Rare-target loss (11.613, 12% of tokens) is dominated by unigram and output-embedding learning at this stage. Recall tokens (13% of targets, 4.475) are the attention-dependent class. Keep rare-token loss as a secondary readout.
qa.decides: which diagnostic the smoke run logs and kills on

qa.q: All 12 layers, or the first few?
qa.a: Unknown which wins. The layer-0 input is the RMS-normed token embedding, because the four streams are identical copies and the read weights sum to 1. So the layer-0 gate is a nonlinear per-token K/V code, freed from the tied input/output embedding geometry. Layer-0 attention gradient is also an outlier (0.24–0.29 vs about 0.02 in its neighbours, z 7.03 on 3 seeds). Build all layers as specified, but log per-layer gate CV to see where the gate is used.
qa.decides: gate in every block vs gate only in block 0 (or blocks 0–1)

qa.q: Should the gate act on the whole shared latent (K and V) or only the V half?
qa.a: The idea keeps one latent shared by K and V, so gating it gates both. K then passes through `k_norm`, which partly absorbs the gate. In Qwen's gated-attention study, gating after the value projection helped less than gating the SDPA output. I recall this from https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.06708 and have not re-checked it. Build the shared gate per spec.
qa.decides: one shared gated latent vs gating only the V slice of `expand` output

qa.q: Which optimizer group does `W_g` land in, and does that matter?
qa.a: It is 2-D and its name contains neither "tok" nor "head", so `build_optimizers` puts it in Muon automatically with shape scale max(1, 128/384)^0.5 = 1. The latent RMSNorm makes the forward pass invariant to the gate's overall scale. Its backward pass amplifies gradients by 1/rms(input), but Muon's orthogonalised update hides gradient scale anyway. No change is needed.
qa.decides: Muon (automatic) vs explicit AdamW

qa.q: Which norms become scalar: only n1/n2/final (which is where the 9,600 count comes from), or also latent_norm, q_norm and k_norm?
qa.a: 12×(384+384)+384 = 9,600, so the stated count covers only the stream read-out norms and the final norm. The "attention temperature at 1.4x" can only live in q_norm/k_norm, because n1's output is renormalized before the content logits. So for the mechanism to exist, the q/k norms must be converted. The faithful build is all 37 norms converted, giving 61 scalars. The stated −9,560 matches neither option and should be corrected to −12,611.
qa.decides: 25 scalars (−9,575) vs 61 scalars (−12,611)

qa.q: What does n1's scalar actually control in this script?
qa.a: `qc` is renormalized by q_norm, and k/v pass through compress→latent_norm, which removes n1's scale. n1's scalar therefore reaches only `qr` (via wq) and `kr` (via `rotary`), so the rotary-part logits scale as s². It is a rotary temperature. Keep it, initialized at 1.0, and name it as such.
qa.decides: keep a scalar on n1 vs make n1 purely no-affine

qa.q: Should the temperature be one learned scalar on q_norm, a scalar on each of q_norm and k_norm, or a fixed `scale=` passed to SDPA?
qa.a: The SDPA default scale is 1/√96, since q is 64+32 wide. With unit gains the maximum content logit is therefore 64/√96 ≈ 6.5, and 1.4x makes it about 9.1. Two scalars multiply into one product and add only redundant gradient scaling. One scalar on q_norm, initialized at 1.4, is the clean build. Caveat: the measured max logits already reach 22.75, which is far above 6.5. The rotary part (or gain growth) likely dominates, so the 1.4x may barely matter (see L2).
qa.decides: one learned scalar per layer, init 1.4, with k_norm no-affine vs two scalars, each init √1.4

qa.q: Should the scalars be weight-decayed?
qa.a: `build_optimizers` sends every non-2-D parameter, including 0-D ones, to AdamW with wd 0.1. The decoupled decay factor over 1,525 steps at lr 3e-3, with a mean LR multiplier of about 0.84, is exp(−0.38) ≈ 0.68 in the absence of gradient. The stated mechanism ("no longer fighting decay") only holds if the scalars are exempt, so add a no-decay group.
qa.decides: leave them in the existing AdamW group (wd 0.1) vs put them in a new no-decay AdamW group

qa.q: Is the final-norm gain redundant?
qa.a: The n1, n2 and latent gains can be absorbed into the next linear layer (a diagonal input scaling), so they are redundant in parameterization. The final gain cannot be absorbed, because the head is tied to `tok`. q/k gains cannot be absorbed either, because they come after the normalization. modded-nanogpt's no-gain evidence comes from an untied head, so it does not cover this case. Whether the gain matters here is unknown. Build it faithfully as a scalar and watch the rare-token bucket (L3).
qa.decides: scalar final norm (faithful) vs keep the 384-wide final gain as an exception

qa.q: How should the scalar be applied?
qa.a: The two are mathematically identical. The expand form keeps a single fused kernel; a stride-0 weight may be copied internally, but that is only d floats. The multiply form adds one elementwise pass, about 3 MB of bf16 per call at micro_batch 4, and saves one activation for backward. Use the expand form. The change in VRAM and step time is well inside C4 either way.
qa.decides: `F.rms_norm(x, (d,), s.expand(d), eps)` vs `F.rms_norm(x, (d,), None, eps) * s`

qa.q: Can a 45-step check with a 0.03 threshold separate signal from noise?
qa.a: At equal seed, the data order is identical, because `Shards` is seeded only by `cfg.seed`. The linear-layer init is also identical, provided the scalars are created with `torch.full` or `torch.tensor` (no RNG draws) and module creation order is unchanged. Paired differences are therefore clean. A single-step loss over 32k tokens still carries a few hundredths of noise, so compare the 10-step mean.
qa.decides: compare loss at step 45 alone vs compare the mean of loss_curve[35:45] on paired seeds

qa.q: Is the proposed TEST ("baseline gains within 10% of uniform → removal safe") informative?
qa.a: Uniform shrinkage from decay is not idleness. A small CV does not prove the gains are unused; it only shows a scalar could replace them. The baseline `model.pt` already contains every gain vector at the full budget, so read the per-vector mean and CV there at no cost. The mean of the baseline's q_norm·k_norm product is the empirically learned temperature, and it should set the init instead of 1.4.
qa.decides: run a separate 500-step probe vs read the gains from an existing full-budget baseline `model.pt`

qa.q: Can removing the gains lower the update-norm spread (the TARGET)?
qa.a: Under Adam, the gains move at roughly lr, about 3e-3, relative to a value of about 1, which is below the 0.020 median. They cannot be the 0.0327 maximum. The spread comes from Muon matrices, where the shape scale reaches √6 for `expand` (768×128). Replace the target.
qa.decides: keep update spread as the success metric vs replace it with entropy plus paired loss

assumes: The per-channel gains act as temperatures and not as feature selectors. In particular, the final norm under a tied head is not doing feature selection.
Muon can learn per-input-channel scaling inside `wq`, `compress`, `rotary`, `w_gate` and `w_up` as cheaply as a diagonal gain trained with Adam.
Attention sharpness is limited by the content-part temperature and not by the unnormalized rotary part.
A temperature of 1.4x is near-optimal at d_head 64 + 32 rotary dims, at 21M parameters and 1,525 steps.
Weight decay on the gains is harmful enough to matter within 1,525 steps.
The scaled branch init (std 0.02/√24 on wo/w_down) stays and does not interact with the scalars.

n1's scale reaches only qr/kr (the rotary logits). latent_norm's scale reaches only v, because k is renormalized by k_norm. n2's scale enters both silu(gate) and up, so the MLP output scales roughly as s².
SDPA uses its default scale of 1/√96 because q/k are 64 content + 32 rotary dims wide.
`read_logits` and `write_logits` are 2-D (2×4) and currently go to Muon; `mix_logits` is 3-D and goes to AdamW. Do not change this in the same build, because it would confound the comparison.
0-D parameters fall into the AdamW "other" group automatically. A new no-decay group requires editing `build_optimizers`.
Full run length: 50e6/32768 = 1,525 steps; warmup 30 steps; cooldown starts at step 1,067.
The scalars must not draw from torch RNG, or the paired-seed init alignment is lost.
Layer-0 attention gradient is 0.24, against about 0.02–0.03 elsewhere (z 7.03, 3 seeds). The likely cause is the tiny raw-embedding stream (std 0.02), and gains do not address it.
Residual RMS grows from 1.403 to 10.893 across depth. Pre-norm read-outs hide this, so the scalars do not see it.

nodes.cluster_name: Per-token scale and bias decoupling norm from direction

qa.q: With zero-init log-scale s and RMS-normalised rows, what is the initial logit scale?
qa.a: RMS-normalised rows have RMS 1, which is 50x the baseline row RMS of 0.02. Logit std becomes about √384 ≈ 19.6 instead of 0.39, and the output gradient into the tied table is also amplified 50x. Zero-init therefore starts at a loss of tens of nats and makes the output side dominate even more, the opposite of the intent. Initialise s = log(0.02) so the head equals the baseline head at step 0, or equivalently L2-normalise and set s = log(0.392).
qa.decides: s init = log(0.02) ≈ −3.91 vs s = 0

qa.q: Can a zero-init learned bias absorb the unigram prior "within the first few hundred steps" under AdamW lr 3e-3?
qa.a: No. Adam moves each element by roughly the learning rate or less per step. That is at most about 0.9 nats by step 300 and about 3.5–4.5 nats over the whole schedule. The log-prior spans more than 10 nats between frequent and rank-10k+ tokens. The prediction in the idea cannot happen with zero init, so take the counted-init variant.
qa.decides: zero-init learned b vs b initialised to counted log-unigram

qa.q: Should s and b be in the AdamW group with weight_decay = 0.1?
qa.a: Decoupled decay costs lr·wd = 3e-4 per step times the value. For b ≈ −10 that is 3e-3 per step toward 0, the same size as the Adam step, and it erases roughly a third of the prior over the run. Decay on s pulls it toward exp(0) = 1, which is a 50x temperature. Put both in a no-decay AdamW group.
qa.decides: the existing `other` group vs a new no-decay group

qa.q: How should the per-token scale and bias be applied without breaking C4?
qa.a: Logits are 4096×50304 in bf16, about 412 MB. Any elementwise operation on them saves at least one more such tensor for backward, which is far beyond the roughly 0.1 GB headroom. Folding adds one 50304×384 bf16 tensor (38.6 MB) plus row statistics. The bias rides in the addmm, so no extra logits-sized tensor is created.
qa.decides: fold into the weight (`W = E * (exp(s) / rms_row(E))[:, None]`, then `F.linear(h, W, b)`) vs elementwise scale/add on the logits

qa.q: Does normalisation beyond the bias change anything the optimiser sees?
qa.a: The output gradient to a raw row becomes (exp(s)/rms)·(I − êêᵀ)g. The radial part is removed exactly, and the tangential part shrinks as rows grow above their initial norm. Under per-element Adam normalisation, magnitudes are partly washed out, so the main surviving effect is the loss of the radial push. Whether that lowers loss is unknown, and it is what the bias-only arm tests.
qa.decides: RMS-normalised direction-only head plus s and b vs bias-only

qa.q: Is "rare-token loss down" the right target?
qa.a: At step 100 the rank-10k+ band sits at 11.6 nats, already above uniform (10.83), so the model is already charging roughly a prior cost there. A correct unigram prior gives rank-10k+ tokens their unigram code length, which is plausibly 12–15 nats (belief). That can raise rare-band loss while lowering total loss. Judge on total loss and the mid bands, and only report the rare band.
qa.decides: rank-10k+ band loss vs total loss plus the 100–10000 bands as the success signal

qa.q: Where are the counts computed?
qa.a: The exam runs GPT(cfg) and then load_state_dict, so counting inside __init__ would read data at exam time and break --build-only. Count in main after the build-only return: - Source: `train.data[0]` with `np.bincount(..., minlength=50304)`. - Smoothing: add-one. The 47 padding ids then get finite, very negative values; avoid −inf in bf16. - Store with `b.copy_(log p)`. Because b is a Parameter, the exam sees it. Never touch val.bin.
qa.decides: inside GPT.__init__ vs in main after the --build-only return

qa.q: Is the steps 30–45 kill window meaningful?
qa.a: Baseline is already at 7.06 by step 26, likely at or below unigram entropy (belief: about 7.3–7.6 nats for GPT-2 BPE on FineWeb-Edu). So steps 30–45 already test whether the head start survives into the bigram phase. However, the 0.02 bar is 4x the C7 margin, and early prior gains routinely fade. Keep 30–45 as the first gate and add a 300-step matched check before any full run. Matched seeds give identical data order, because the Shards RNG is independent of the model.
qa.decides: kill on steps 30–45 vs kill on a matched window at about steps 250–300

qa.q: Does the bias interact with global grad clipping at 1.0?
qa.a: Unknown magnitude. The bias gradient is mean(p − onehot) over 32k tokens. Its norm is up to about 1 when the prior is wrong and small when it is counted. With counted init it should rarely trigger clipping. Log the pre-clip global norm in both arms.
qa.decides: include s and b in clip_grad_norm_ vs clip them separately or exclude them

qa.q: Does the tied head's self-logit (the token scoring itself through its own embedding in the residual) get worse?
qa.a: Sinkhorn mixing is doubly stochastic, so the mean over streams preserves the input exactly: the readout always contains e_x plus the branch writes. With s = log(rms0), the self-logit at init equals baseline (about 7.7). Later, as raw rows grow on the input side but not in the head, the ratio drifts in an unmeasured direction. Measure the logit of the current token in both arms.
qa.decides: plain readout vs readout that subtracts tok(idx)

nodes.focus: Have induction heads formed by 1.5M or 3.3M tokens at this scale?

qa.q: Which training steps do 1.5M and 3.3M tokens correspond to, and where do they sit in the LR schedule?
qa.a: With `batch_tokens` 32768 there are 1525 total steps. Step 45 is 1.47M tokens and step 100 is 3.28M. Warmup ends at step 30 (`int(1525·0.02)`), so by step 45 the model has had only about 15 steps at full learning rate. Both checkpoints sit at 3–7% of the run.
qa.decides: kill check at step 45 vs a later kill check (≥ step 300)

qa.q: Does the measured recall-token gap at step 100 (4.475 vs 6.704) show that induction heads exist?
qa.a: No. The split is confounded. Recall targets lean toward frequent tokens and repeated phrases. They can also be lowered by a skip-trigram head that boosts "any earlier token in the window", which is not induction. Without a frequency-matched control, the 2.2-nat gap does not show prefix-matching.
qa.decides: recall metric = "bigram already seen in window" split vs a repeated-random-token in-context score

qa.q: What does published work say about when induction heads form?
qa.a: Olsson et al. find a sharp phase change in small models early in training, at roughly 2.5–5B tokens (https://transformer-circuits.pub/2022/in-context-learning-and-induction-heads/index.html). That is about 1000× more than 3.3M tokens. Their setup used Adam and a different schedule. Muon-trained speedrun models learn much faster per token, but I know of no published measurement putting natural-text induction formation below about 10M tokens. For this exact configuration the answer is unknown.
qa.decides: kill check at step 45/100 vs a check placed after a measured formation step

qa.q: Is the model's loss at step 45/100 in the regime where induction usually appears?
qa.a: The mixed loss at step 100 is 0.13·4.475 + 0.87·6.704 ≈ 6.41 nats. That is near unigram-level prediction; GPT-2 BPE unigram entropy on web text is roughly 7.3–7.5 nats (my estimate, unchecked). Induction emerges after bigram statistics are learned, at far lower loss. At step 45 the loss is higher still, so the model is still in the unigram/bigram phase.
qa.decides: kill check at step 45/100 vs at a loss threshold (e.g. first step with total loss < 4.5)

qa.q: Does the precondition exist: a sharp previous-token head in an early layer?
qa.a: The measured layer-0 entropy is 0.957 and the minimum across layers is 0.667. Neither is a sharp δ=1 head. Telling δ=1 from δ=2 in the shared 32-dim rotary key needs the fast frequencies. The step at which those entropies were measured is not in the brief, which leaves this unknown. If they were measured at step 100, the previous-token head that K-composition needs has not formed, so induction cannot have formed either.
qa.decides: rotate the fast frequencies (k=0..15 over the 32 dims) vs only the slow band (16 dims, k=8..15)

qa.q: Before induction forms, does the value rotation cost capacity?
qa.a: Yes, this is the expected outcome. With near-uniform attention over T positions, |Σ a_ij e^{iωδ}| ≈ 1/(Tω) for fast ω. The fast-frequency rotated dims therefore cancel to almost nothing, and half of each value head is close to dead early on. At step 45 the idea pays its L2 cost and has nothing to gain from L4. The kill rule's "total loss above baseline" clause is biased toward a false kill.
qa.decides: rotate from step 0 vs rotate only after the attention sharpens (ramp or delayed switch)

qa.q: Does an induction head need the offset carried in its value at all?
qa.a: Not for its own prediction. An induction head's value is the copied token's content, and the offset of the attended token does not change what gets copied. A plausible benefit is upstream instead. A diffuse early head whose output encodes the offset in its phase could hand later layers previous-token information, speeding up induction formation. That benefit would show up as an earlier formation step, not as lower recall loss at a fixed step.
qa.decides: rotate values in all layers vs only in early layers (1–3), where the offset can feed previous-token / K-composition

qa.q: What cheap measurement settles formation at this scale?
qa.a: Train the baseline once and save `state_dict` at steps 45, 100, 200, 400, 800 and 1525. This is a separate probe script, not the harness file. Feed 8×(256 random tokens repeated twice) and measure the loss drop of the second copy against the first. Also compute the per-head prefix-matching score. Formation is the first step where the in-context drop exceeds about 1 nat and some head scores above 0.3. This costs one baseline run of compute.
qa.decides: 45-step matched smoke vs a checkpoint-sweep probe before any A/B

qa.q: Does this architecture (MLA latent 128, shared rotary key, 4-stream Sinkhorn mixing) delay induction compared with a plain GPT?
qa.a: Unknown. Two mechanisms could delay it: - Every head's key content passes through one 128-dim latent shared by 6 heads × (k and v). Previous-token information must survive that compression to be used in K-composition. - The single shared rotary key means all 6 heads see identical positional keys, so per-head positional specialisation comes only from the queries.
qa.decides: keep the shared rotary key vs give each head its own rotary key dims for the test

qa.q: Which frequency band carries offset information inside a 1024 window without cancelling?
qa.a: The wavelength is 2π·10000^(k/16). For k ≥ 12 it is ≥ 6283 tokens, so the rotation over 1024 tokens stays below about 1 rad: little offset information, but little cancellation. For k ≤ 2 (wavelength < 20) it cancels almost completely under diffuse attention. The useful band is roughly k = 3..10 (about 35–1990 tokens). Because `apply_rope` pairs `x[:d]` with `x[d:]`, a 16-dim band must use the matching 8 columns of `cos`/`sin`.
qa.decides: rotate `v[..., :32]` with all 16 frequencies vs a 16-dim band using `cos[:, k0:k0+8]`

qa.q: Does the loss depend on `mix_logits` at all while `read_logits` are uniform?
qa.a: No. Sinkhorn ends with a column normalisation, so the column sums are exactly 1 in fp32 and the stream mean is invariant to M. Every read with uniform weights and the final `x.mean(dim=2)` read only the mean. So the forward pass is independent of M, and the gradient to `mix_logits` is zero up to bf16 rounding until the read logits move.
qa.decides: rank the sweep by 45-step smoke loss vs rank it by a stream diagnostic or by full runs.

qa.q: Which way does a lower temperature move the differences between streams?
qa.a: At init, M = aI + b(J − I), with eigenvalue 1 on the mean and a − b on every difference direction. - The per-stage factor a − b is 0.990 at init 6, 0.827 at init 3, 0.615 at init 2 and 0.30 at init 1. - Over 24 stages this compounds to 0.79, 0.010, 8.6e-6 and about 3e-13. - So inits of 2 or lower wipe out stream differences within a few blocks. The model then collapses to a single residual stream, which is the opposite of the stated mechanism.
qa.decides: sweep {1, 2, 3, 6} vs sweep only {3, 4, 6} or switch to a non-contracting mix.

qa.q: Can streams 2 and 3 ever differ?
qa.a: No (belief, from symmetry). - Both streams start as the same embedding copy and have identical write logits (−0.01 in both stages) and identical read logits. - The mix logits are symmetric under swapping 2 and 3, so the forward pass is equivariant under that swap. - Their gradients and updates are therefore identical, and they stay clones for the whole run. The design is effectively 3 streams, and no temperature fixes this.
qa.decides: keep the current `write_logits` init vs give all four streams distinct read and write inits.

qa.q: Which optimiser updates the stream logits, and what does weight decay do to them?
qa.a: Placement follows from the `ndim` filter in `build_optimizers`: - **`mix_logits` (2,4,4):** 3-D, so it goes to AdamW at 3e-3 with weight decay 0.1. Decay alone multiplies the diagonal by exp(−0.1·3e-3·~1281 effective steps) ≈ 0.68. That takes init 6 to about 4.1 (1.6% off-diagonal) and init 2 to about 1.36 (14.5% off-diagonal), so decay is already a hidden temperature schedule. - **`read_logits` and `write_logits` (2,4):** 2-D, so they go to Muon at lr 0.02 with weight decay 0.1. Newton–Schulz rescales the update to unit spectral norm, so even tiny gradients produce updates of about 0.01 per e
qa.decides: leave the stream logits in the current groups vs a separate AdamW group with weight decay 0.

qa.q: Can a 45-step smoke run rank the inits?
qa.a: No. - Warmup lasts 30 steps, so by step 45 the read logits have moved only about 0.2. The effect of M is then second order (read deviation × stream spread) and is swamped by rounding and seed noise. - C7 asks for a gap above 0.005 nats at p < 0.01, which only full runs can show. - A same-seed smoke sweep is useful only as a sanity check that the loss curves are nearly identical.
qa.decides: smoke sweep vs going straight to full-length runs of two values.

qa.q: Does the 4-stream design beat the single-stream baseline at all?
qa.a: Unknown; nothing in the brief measures it. At 1B scale, static ×4 hyper-connections gave a small gain over the baseline, and dynamic ×4 did better (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2409.19606). Because low temperature converges to single-stream behaviour (A2), a neutral 4-stream result implies a neutral sweep.
qa.decides: spend runs on temperature vs first ablate to n = 1.

qa.q: Does the mixing push the residual through bf16?
qa.a: Belief, not run. - Under autocast the einsum lowers to bmm, which runs in bf16. The carried residual is therefore rounded to bf16 at all 24 stages, even though the write addition promotes back to fp32. - After the bf16 cast, column sums are off by about 4–5e-4 at both init 6 and init 2. That shrinks the mean by roughly 1% over depth. Temperature barely changes this, but it adds noise to any comparison.
qa.decides: compute the mix in fp32 with autocast disabled vs leave it as is.

qa.q: Can the final readout use stream differences?
qa.a: No. `x.mean(dim=2)` is invariant to M and to how the signal is spread across streams. Only the 24 intermediate reads can exploit differences, which caps what any mixing temperature can buy.
qa.decides: keep the mean readout vs a learned softmax final read.

qa.q: Where does the literature say Birkhoff-constrained mixing ends up, and has a lower init been tested?
qa.a: Neither paper tested a lower init. - sHC reports that mHC matrices collapse toward identity and that non-negativity blocks subtractive mixing (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2603.20896). - The stream-collapse paper reports that the mix stays near identity while one stream dominates, and that a symmetry-breaking init helps (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2606.03483).
qa.decides: lower init vs a symmetry-breaking init.

qa.q: Does the 20-iteration Sinkhorn cost matter for step time, and does the init change it?
qa.a: The init does not change the cost. - Each optimizer step runs about 40 tiny kernels per stage × 24 stages × 8 micro-batches forward, plus the backward, although M depends only on the parameters. The wall-time share on the 4050 is unmeasured. - At init, M is a symmetric circulant matrix, so Sinkhorn is a no-op there.
qa.decides: 20 iterations per forward vs an exact parameterisation or mixing at fewer stages.

nodes.focus: At which step does the baseline form induction heads (repeated-random gain > 1 nat)?

qa.q: Has the baseline's repeated-random gain been measured at any step?
qa.a: Unknown. No such measurement is in the brief, and the script saves no mid-run checkpoints. Today the onset step is a guess, not a number.
qa.decides: keep the 45/100-step kill vs replace it with a kill placed after a measured onset

qa.q: Does the published induction onset transfer to this run's token budget?
qa.a: Not directly. Olsson et al. put the phase change at about 2.5–5B tokens (https://transformer-circuits.pub/2022/in-context-learning-and-induction-heads/index.html). That is 50–100x this run's 50M budget, and it used Adam, a different model and different data. Muon and a high LR could pull the onset much earlier, but by how much here is unknown.
qa.decides: expect induction inside 1525 steps vs treat this run as pre-induction throughout

qa.q: Can the onset land at or before step 45 or 100, where the kill check sits?
qa.a: Very unlikely. - Step 100 is only 3.28M tokens. The model is still about 4.4 nats below uniform and dominated by unigram/bigram fitting (measured: mixed loss 6.41). - Every layer is diffuse (entropy 0.667–0.957), with no sharp head, so there is no previous-token head for an induction head to compose with. - A recall-loss kill at step 45 therefore tests noise, not the mechanism.
qa.decides: kill at step 45 vs kill at the end of the run (or at the measured onset + 100 steps)

qa.q: How should checkpoints be produced without touching the harness file's contract?
qa.a: Use a separate probe script outside the harness. It imports `GPT`, `Config`, `Shards`, `build_optimizers` and `lr_mult`, runs the same loop, and saves `state_dict` in bf16 every 50 steps. - Each checkpoint is about 81 MB (40.56M params × 2 bytes), so ~31 checkpoints ≈ 2.5 GB per seed. - Every 100 steps (16 checkpoints) halves that and still resolves the onset to within 3.3M tokens. - The harness file stays unchanged (C5).
qa.decides: separate probe script that imports the trainer vs adding a checkpoint flag to the harness file

qa.q: Does the cooldown (steps 1067–1525) shift the onset?
qa.a: Unknown for this setup. LR annealing generally sharpens attention, so a pre-induction run at step 1066 could cross 1 nat during cooldown. Measure at both points.
qa.decides: check the kill once, before cooldown, vs at two points (step 1066 and step 1525)

qa.q: Does the value-rotation mechanism actually need induction heads, or would previous-token heads suffice to show it?
qa.a: The canonical induction circuit does not need offset in the value. It needs: - a previous-token head, which writes the prior token's identity, and - a query–key match on that identity. Offset in the value mainly helps tell copies at different distances apart. So the mechanism's first observable is more likely in previous-token and local heads, which form before induction. The probe should log the per-layer mean attention mass at offset 1 next to the repeated-random gain.
qa.decides: target metric = recall-token loss vs previous-token-head score (attention mass at offset 1)

qa.q: Is the 1-nat threshold informative at this loss level?
qa.a: The threshold is too coarse alone. A full induction circuit gives gains of several nats on repeated random tokens, and partial bigram copying can pass 1 nat without true induction. Report the full curve and the step of steepest gain rise; the 1-nat crossing stays as a secondary marker.
qa.decides: report the onset as a single threshold step vs report the full gain curve plus the step of maximum slope

qa.q: How much does the onset vary across seeds?
qa.a: Unknown here. Phase changes are sharp but their timing jitters across seeds. Use 3 seeds, matching the 3-seed layer-0 gradient measurement already on record.
qa.decides: 1 probe seed vs 3 probe seeds before fixing the kill step

qa.q: Could this architecture delay induction relative to a plain GPT?
qa.a: Unknown, but there are concrete reasons it might: - The rotary key `kr` is a single 32-dim vector shared by all 6 heads. Previous-token heads must therefore share one positional key and can only differ through `qr`. - The SDPA scale is 1/sqrt(96), which damps the 32 positional dims against the 64 content dims. - Both factors could slow the formation of sharp positional heads.
qa.decides: probe the baseline as-is vs also probe a plain-MHA reference to separate architecture from optimizer effects

nodes.focus: What per-vector CV and mean do the baseline's n1/n2/final/q/k gains end with at the full budget?

qa.q: Do the baseline's saved `model.pt` files already hold the answer, so no new training is needed?
qa.a: Unknown whether the harness kept them. If it did, `state_dict` holds `blocks.{i}.n1.weight`, `n2.weight`, `attn.latent_norm.weight`, `attn.q_norm.weight`, `attn.k_norm.weight` and `norm.weight` for every seed. Reading them costs nothing and fully settles mean and CV at the full budget. Nothing in the material above contains these numbers.
qa.decides: read gains from the existing baseline checkpoints vs spend 3 new full baseline runs on measurement

qa.q: How much CV does a gain vector reach from gradient noise alone under this optimizer?
qa.a: The gains sit in AdamW with lr 3e-3 and eps 1e-10. With eps that small, Adam is nearly sign-normalized, so even a channel with a tiny, signal-free gradient moves at the full rate. The random-walk displacement is about 3e-3·√(Σ mult²) = 3e-3·√1200.7 ≈ 0.104 at the full budget, or about 0.09 after decay shrinks the early steps. Pure noise therefore gives a CV of about 0.10–0.13. The 10% test threshold sits at or below the noise floor and cannot tell an idle gain from a used one.
qa.decides: the idea's "within 10% of uniform means idle" threshold vs a threshold calibrated against the noise floor (about 0.2)

qa.q: How far does weight decay alone move the mean?
qa.a: The norms are 1-D, so they land in AdamW with weight_decay 0.1. The schedule gives 15.5 + 1037 + 229.5 = 1282 effective full-lr steps. With no gradient, the factor is exp(−3e-4·1282) = 0.681, and it is 0.864 by step 500. Decay is real, but it is weak next to Adam's step size. Equilibrium only needs the gradient signal-to-noise ratio m/√v ≥ 0.1·w, which a scalar (a sum over channels) meets far more easily than a single channel.
qa.decides: put the scalars in the decayed AdamW "other" group vs add a no-decay group in `build_optimizers`

qa.q: Which gain vectors are functionally redundant, and which are not?
qa.a: The n1, n2 and latent_norm gains feed straight into Linear layers (wq/compress/rotary, w_gate/w_up, expand). Their per-channel values are exactly absorbable as column scales of those matrices, so they matter only for optimization: they give Adam a diagonal preconditioner that Muon's orthogonalized updates cannot produce. The q_norm/k_norm gains, and the final gain under tied embeddings, are not absorbable. They set the logit geometry directly.
qa.decides: the 25-scalar set (n1, n2, final) vs the 61-scalar set (every RMSNorm instance)

qa.q: Where must the "1.4x attention temperature" scalar sit to actually reach q·k?
qa.a: The overall scale of n1 cancels in qc (q_norm), k (k_norm) and v (latent_norm). It survives only in qr and kr, both of which come from n1, so an n1 scalar s scales the rotary logits by s² and leaves the content logits untouched. A 1.4x content temperature therefore needs a scalar on q_norm (or k_norm). q_norm is outside the 9,600-parameter set the idea names, so the 25-scalar build cannot deliver L2.
qa.decides: scalar on q_norm (content temperature) vs scalar on n1 (rotary temperature only)

qa.q: Which statistic of the q/k gains is meaningful?
qa.a: The content logit depends only on the per-channel product gq⊙gk. Each 64-vector is shared across all 6 heads of its layer, because RMSNorm(64) acts on the last dimension. The individual vectors can drift along gq·gk = const, with decay pulling them toward gq = gk. The CV of each vector alone is therefore ambiguous: measure the CV and mean of the product. One scalar on q captures the whole temperature; a second scalar on k is a redundant direction.
qa.decides: one temperature scalar on q only vs a scalar on both q and k

qa.q: Does a 500-step probe predict the full-budget end state?
qa.a: No. At step 500 the noise CV is about 0.066 and the decay factor 0.864. At the end they are about 0.10 and 0.681. Any real per-channel drift also keeps growing during the 1,037 flat steps. A 500-step measurement underestimates both mean drift and CV, so the open question requires the full budget, or Q1's checkpoints.
qa.decides: a 500-step baseline probe vs a full 1,525-step probe

qa.q: How do you tell feature selection from temperature in the end state, beyond CV?
qa.a: Count the channels with |g| < 0.2·mean and check for sign flips, since Adam can push a gain negative. Then mean-ablate each vector in the checkpoint (replace it by its mean) and measure the loss change on train-shard windows split by token-frequency bucket. Never use val. For the absorbable gains (n1/n2/latent), ablation overstates their importance because the downstream matrices co-adapted. For the final and q/k gains, the ablation delta is the direct answer.
qa.decides: convert the final norm to a scalar vs keep the final gain vector

qa.q: What should the scalars be initialized to?
qa.a: Unknown until Q1 or the probe is answered. Initializing at 1.0 keeps step-0 behavior identical to the baseline, so it preserves the paired comparison. Initializing at the end-state mean (if it differs from 1 by more than 0.2) removes a drift the scalar would otherwise spend early steps on. Either way, `torch.tensor(value)` draws no RNG.
qa.decides: init 1.0 (the current start) vs init to the baseline's end-of-run mean

qa.q: Muon decays matrices hard. Do the gains carry the scales Muon cannot hold?
qa.a: Muon's decay alone would give exp(−0.02·0.1·1282) = exp(−2.56) ≈ 0.077, so Muon matrix scale sits at an lr/wd equilibrium that ignores the gradient. That leaves the n2 gain as the free knob for the gate pre-activation scale, and the q/k gains as the only knob for content temperature. This supports the idea's premise that the temperatures matter. It also predicts that baseline n2 and q/k means drift away from 1, a belief not yet measured.
qa.decides: a plain scalar vs a Gemma-style (1+w) vector that decays toward identity

nodes.cluster_name: Per-token scale and bias decoupling norm from direction
nodes.focus: What is the matched-seed noise of a 15-step mean loss across seeds, and can a 0.005 bias-only margin be resolved with 3 seeds?

qa.q: Does a 45-step smoke run reproduce the full run's learning-rate schedule at steps 30–45?
qa.a: No. With `--smoke-steps 45`, `lr_mult` gets warm = max(1, int(0.9)) = 1 and cool_start = int(31.5) = 31. So indices 31–44 decay linearly from 1.0 to 1/14, and the KILL window would be mostly annealed loss. In the full run, warm = 30 and cool_start = 1067, so steps 30–45 are the first full-LR steps. `--smoke-seconds` keeps total_steps = 1525 and only breaks on time, so its `loss_curve[:45]` matches the full run step for step. Use it, with a time budget that covers at least 45 steps, and read `loss_curve[29:45]`.
qa.decides: `--smoke-steps 45` vs `--smoke-seconds` cutoff with the 1525-step schedule left in place

qa.q: Do arms with the same seed see identical batches?
qa.a: Yes, provided the build keeps them identical. `Shards` draws from its own `np.random.default_rng(seed)`, which only `sample()` consumes, so batch k is the same in every arm with the same seed. Torch init is also identical as long as s and b are created with `torch.zeros`/`torch.full` (no RNG calls). The counted prior must be computed from a fixed slice, for example the first N tokens of `train_000`, never through `train.rng`. Under these conditions, batch-content noise cancels in the per-seed arm difference.
qa.decides: paired same-seed differencing vs pooled unpaired Welch for the KILL rule

qa.q: Is a same-seed rerun bitwise reproducible, so that the paired noise floor is zero?
qa.a: Unknown. The tied table receives an embedding-backward gradient and an SDPA backward gradient, and PyTorch lists several CUDA backward ops as nondeterministic (https://pytorch.org/docs/stable/notes/randomness.html). Under bf16 and Muon at full LR, any bit difference will grow. Two same-seed baseline reruns give the paired floor directly: the sd of their `mean(loss_curve[29:45])` difference.
qa.decides: measure the floor with A/A same-seed reruns vs force `torch.use_deterministic_algorithms(True)` for the probe runs

qa.q: What is the across-seed sd of the 15-step mean training loss?
qa.a: Unknown here. It can be computed at no cost from the three existing baseline seeds' `loss_curve` (the layer-0 gradient measurement already used 3 seeds). My belief: 32 windows per step with a window-level loss sd of about 0.4–0.5 nats gives about 0.07–0.09 per step. Seed-dependent data then makes the 15-step mean sd about 0.015–0.025 nats, plus init variance.
qa.decides: an unpaired 3+3 Welch kill vs a paired or longer-window kill

qa.q: What sd would let 3 seeds resolve a 0.005 margin?
qa.a: Unpaired Welch with 3+3 and equal variance has df ≈ 4 and t₀.₉₉ = 3.747. SE = 0.816·s, so it needs s < 0.0016 nats, which is about 10× below my belief in A4. That is not resolvable. Paired with n = 3 (df 2, t₀.₉₉ = 6.965) needs sd_d < 0.00124. With n = 5 (t = 3.747) it needs sd_d < 0.0030; with n = 8 (t = 2.998), sd_d < 0.0047. Three seeds resolve 0.005 only if the A/A floor from A3 is about 0.001 or less.
qa.decides: 3 seeds vs 5–8 seeds (or a paired design)

qa.q: Is the logged loss precise enough to see 0.005?
qa.a: Probably yes. `log_softmax`/`nll_loss` are on autocast's float32 list (https://pytorch.org/docs/stable/amp.html), so the loss should be fp32, and `loss_curve` rounds to 1e-4. If it were bf16, the grid spacing in the 4–8 range would be 0.031. Print `loss.dtype` once to confirm.
qa.decides: use `loss.item()` as is vs log an explicit fp32 loss

qa.q: Is steps 30–45 the right phase for the bias-only vs direction-only margin?
qa.a: Probably not for L4. The baseline is already at 7.06 by step 26, which I believe is below the GPT-2-token unigram entropy of about 7.5 nats (unchecked). The unigram prior is therefore largely learned by step 30, and any bias advantage there is a transient. The representation effect that L4 claims would show later, and the A/A noise floor also grows with step count. Both windows need the A3 measurement.
qa.decides: KILL window 30–45 vs a later window (e.g. 200–300 at full LR)

qa.q: Does the bias gradient change grad clipping, confounding the comparison against the baseline?
qa.a: Possibly. `clip_grad_norm_` covers every parameter, and b's gradient (mean softmax minus empirical frequency) has norm up to √2. Whenever the baseline's total norm is near 1, adding b scales down every other update. This is shared by bias-only and direction-only, but it confounds the comparison with the baseline. Log the value `clip_grad_norm_` returns in all arms.
qa.decides: clip over all params vs exclude s and b from `clip_grad_norm_`

qa.q: Should the readout be the training-loss window or a fixed probe set?
qa.a: A fixed probe gives a paired, step-free readout plus per-band rare-token losses for L4 at no extra cost. Example: 64 windows from the tail of the last `train_*.bin`; the sampler's overlap with them is negligible, and val is never touched (C6). However, smoke runs save no `model.pt`, so the probe has to live in the script (train-only) or a separate tool needs a weights dump. Unknown which the harness tolerates.
qa.decides: `loss_curve[29:45]` mean vs a fixed probe of train windows evaluated after step 45

qa.q: Must the bias-only arm share the direction-only arm's bias init?
qa.a: Yes. L1 predicts that counted vs zero init alone moves step-26 loss by 0.03–0.3. That is 6–60× the 0.005 margin, so mismatched inits make the KILL test measure init instead of normalization. Use counted init in both arms, or zero in both.
qa.decides: zero-init bias-only vs counted-init bias-only as the comparison arm

nodes.cluster_name: Slow batch-level gain on MLP write

qa.q: In this pre-norm stack, can absolute residual RMS affect loss at all, or only the ratio of each write to the accumulated stream?
qa.a: Every read goes through an RMSNorm (`n1`, `n2`, final `norm`), so a global rescale of the stream does not change the logits. Only the relative share of each write matters: the share of late layers shrinks as the stream grows. Whether that shrinking costs loss at this scale is unknown. If the mechanism is real, the relative target is the one that acts on it.
qa.decides: absolute target (write RMS = exp(a)) vs relative target (write RMS = exp(a)·ema of block-input stream RMS)

qa.q: Under AGC, will Muon grow the MLP matrices less (as predicted) or more?
qa.a: Probably more. With a detached EMA, each step's gradient still contains a "make the output bigger" radial component. Muon applies fixed-size updates regardless of gradient scale, so ||W|| keeps growing while the EMA cancels the effect on the output. That is the scale-invariant norm-growth effect, with effective step size falling as ||W|| grows (https://arxiv.org/abs/1803.01814, https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.05350). Weight decay 0.1·lr is the only brake. This is unmeasured, so log ||W||.
qa.decides: leave W free vs add a norm constraint or extra weight decay on the MLP matrices

qa.q: Can a move far enough under the shared AdamW group (lr 3e-3, wd 0.1)?
qa.a: Probably not. Adam moves a by at most about lr per step: roughly 0.12 nats over 45 steps and about 4 nats over the whole 1525-step run. In the baseline, writes go from about 0.01 (init) to O(1) by step 100, about 4.6 nats. A gain-1 init would leave the MLP nearly silenced early while attention writes grow freely. Give a its own group with lr around 0.03–0.1 and no weight decay. Weight decay would also pull a toward 0, i.e. gain 1/ema.
qa.decides: a in the existing "other" group vs its own group (higher lr, no weight decay)

qa.q: How should a and the EMA be initialised?
qa.a: Estimated initial write RMS is about 0.01. Inputs are normalized to RMS 1; w_gate/w_up std 0.02 gives pre-activation std of about 0.39; silu·up gives about 0.077; w_down std 0.00408 over 1077 inputs gives about 0.010. So a = 0 means gain ≈ 100, which trips the idea's own kill bound (>50) at step 1. Use lazy init: a sentinel EMA value replaced via `torch.where` on the first training forward (no `.item()` sync), and a = log(target), where the target comes from Q3/Q11.
qa.decides: a = 0 vs a = log(first measured write RMS); EMA analytic init vs lazy init on the first training forward

qa.q: What EMA momentum, and updated per micro-batch or per optimizer step?
qa.a: Early Muon relative updates are large. For w_down: lr 0.02 × ||orthogonal update||_F ≈ √384 ≈ 19.6 gives 0.39 per step against an init norm of 2.6, about 15% per step. Growth at rate r with lag τ leaves a constant overshoot of e^{rτ}. A 12-step window (0.99 per micro-batch with 8 micro-batches per step) could overshoot several-fold during warmup. Use about 0.9 per micro-batch, or bias-corrected momentum that ramps up. "Slow" is safe only after the warmup phase.
qa.decides: momentum 0.9 vs 0.99 per micro-batch; update every micro-batch vs once per step

qa.q: Does the exam call `model.eval()` or run under `no_grad`?
qa.a: Unknown. Gate on both, and register the EMA as a persistent buffer so `model.pt` carries it. Otherwise the exam would update statistics on validation tokens and make results depend on batch order.
qa.decides: gate EMA updates on `self.training` only vs on `self.training and torch.is_grad_enabled()`

qa.q: Should the current batch's statistic enter the scale used for that same batch?
qa.a: Update-then-use computes the RMS over all 1024 positions, so future tokens leak a tiny amount into earlier positions' scale. That is a causal violation, even if small, and train and eval would differ. Use the previous EMA, then update.
qa.decides: use the previous EMA, then update vs update, then use

qa.q: Does the idea's kill bound on gain, exp(a)/ema ∈ [0.02, 50], fire by construction?
qa.a: Likely. Raw output scales roughly with the product of three matrix norms. By step 45, raw growth is somewhere between about 1.6x (random-walk updates) and about 45x (aligned updates). The baseline reaching residual RMS 1.4 by step 100 suggests the aligned end. With a pinned (Q3), the gain falls toward or below 0.02 with the output still healthy. The bound measures W growth, not failure.
qa.decides: keep the absolute-gain kill vs redefine it as gain relative to its step-0 value, or as write RMS / exp(a)

qa.q: Are MLP writes or attention writes the bigger part of the stream growth?
qa.a: Unmeasured. Layer 0 shows anomalous gradients in both sublayers (attention 0.29, MLP 0.23, z 7.0 and 5.8). Log per-sublayer write RMS in the baseline before building; if attention dominates, L2 cannot hold.
qa.decides: AGC on the MLP only (as specified) vs MLP plus attention

qa.q: How should the 45-step test match the baseline?
qa.a: `lr_mult` scales with total steps. At 45 steps, warmup is 1 step and cooldown starts at step 31. At 100 steps, warmup is 2 steps and cooldown starts at 70. A 45-step run is therefore not matched to the 100-step baseline curve. Run 100 steps (or rerun the baseline at 45) and compare steps 40–45.
qa.decides: `--smoke-steps 45` vs a 100-step run read at steps 40–45

qa.q: Should the EMA track mean-square or RMS, and in what precision?
qa.a: Track sqrt(ema(mean y²)) in fp32. It is the unbiased envelope and avoids bf16 rounding across 12 layers × 8 micro-batches. Compute exp(a)/ema in fp32 and cast the scalar to `y.dtype`.
qa.decides: sqrt(ema(mean y²)) in fp32 vs ema(rms) in bf16

Fixing the residual growth does not change the loss.** Every consumer of the stream is behind an RMSNorm (`n1`, `n2`, final `norm`, plus `q_norm`/`k_norm`), so absolute stream scale only matters as a ratio between writers. The baseline grows MLP writes so that deep layers stay audible against the ac

The 1.403→10.893 figure is the stream after each whole block, with the MLP share unmeasured. If attention writes carry most of the growth, the stream ratio stays at x7

Only helps early.** The x7.8 growth was measured at step 100, the high-LR transient. Over the 30% linear cooldown to lr=0 both arms settle, so any early edge from bounded writes shrinks by the end. The 40–45 step kill test cannot see this decay

Exam-time buffer handling.** The harness rebuilds `GPT(cfg)` and loads `model.pt`. If the EMA is registered with `persistent=False`, it loads at its init value (for example 1.0) instead of about 0.01, and every MLP write is off by about 75x, which is catastrophic. A momentum chosen "per step" lags 8x less than intended, and the batch-noise in c rises. An EMA initialized at 0 without bia

nodes.focus: What are the end-of-run mean and CV per vector of n1, n2, latent, gq⊙gk, and final across the 3 baseline seeds?

qa.q: Do three end-of-run baseline `model.pt` files (seeds 0–2, this exact MLA + 4-stream script) already exist, or must the baseline be rerun to read the gains?
qa.a: Unknown. None of the material provided reports a checkpoint path or gain values. The statistics need only the parameters and no data, so a dump at the end of training is legal under C6 and costs nothing at run time. It is still a training-script edit and must not land in the candidate build.
qa.decides: measure offline from existing checkpoints vs add a `norm_stats` dump to `metrics.json` and rerun 3 baselines

qa.q: What CV would a gain vector reach with no useful gradient at all, which is the noise floor the measured CV must be compared against?
qa.a: AdamW applied to pure-noise gradients random-walks each channel with std ≈ lr·√Σmult² = 3e-3·√1200.7 ≈ 0.104, while decay shrinks the mean to exp(−0.1·3e-3·1282) ≈ 0.681. Noise alone therefore gives CV ≈ 0.10–0.15 per vector. "CV < 0.15" cannot separate an idle vector from a slightly used one, so the rule has to change.
qa.decides: keep the L4 rule "CV < 0.15 means idle" vs replace it with an ablation-based rule

qa.q: Can channel-wise statistics be pooled or correlated across the 3 seeds?
qa.a: No. Residual-stream and head-dim bases come from seed-dependent random init, so channel i in seed 0 has no relation to channel i in seed 1. Cross-seed agreement can only be checked on permutation-invariant summaries: mean, CV, robust CV (MAD/median), min, max, and the sorted gain profile.
qa.decides: report a cross-seed per-channel correlation vs report only per-vector summaries plus a within-seed ablation

qa.q: For n1, n2 and latent_norm, does the measured CV matter for expressivity at all?
qa.a: It does not. Each of these gains multiplies the input of a following Linear layer, so it can be folded exactly into that layer's columns, and removing it loses no function. What remains differs only in optimization dynamics, which a scalar affects through how fast the overall scale can move. Their mean matters more than their CV. In particular, the n1 mean sets only the rotary-logit temperature (s²).
qa.decides: convert these three to one scalar each vs make them fully weightless (no scalar)

qa.q: What is the baseline mean of gq⊙gk per layer, and does the 1.4× init matter by the end of the run?
qa.a: The mean is unknown. A scalar's gradient aggregates over every channel, so its Adam step runs close to the full lr when the gradient sign is consistent. Moving 0.4 then takes about 0.4 / 3e-3 ≈ 133 full-lr steps. The init can therefore shape only roughly steps 0–150, and the final temperature is set by the gradient/decay equilibrium, not by the init. The noise floor of the product is higher than that of a single vector: √(0.10² + 0.13²) gives roughly 0.14–0.18.
qa.decides: q-side scalar initialized to 1.4 vs 1.0

qa.q: Is the final-norm gain the one vector that carries real per-channel information, given that it is the only untied per-channel freedom between the input and output embeddings?
qa.a: Unknown. It is decided by mean-ablation, not by CV: replace g_final with mean(g_final) in each seed's checkpoint and measure the Δ train loss on held-out train-shard windows, split by frequency bucket (rank 0–100 vs 10000+). Keep the vector if the rare-bucket Δ exceeds 0.05. Keeping it costs about 383 params of the saving.
qa.decides: convert the final norm to a scalar vs keep its 384-wide gain as the one exception

qa.q: Are the CVs dominated by a few outlier channels (near-zero or very large gains), which would mean feature selection rather than temperature?
qa.a: Unknown. Report min, max, robust CV and the count of channels below 0.2·mean or above 3·mean, alongside the plain CV. If any vector has outlier channels, the L4 break condition "channels near 0" is met and that norm keeps its gain.
qa.decides: uniform scalar everywhere vs scalar plus a frozen per-channel mask for outlier channels

qa.q: Do mean and CV vary systematically with depth, especially at layer 0, where the attention gradient is 0.24 against 0.02–0.03 elsewhere?
qa.a: Unknown. Layer 0 is already known to behave differently (z 7.03 over 3 seeds), so per-layer scalars are the safer default (24 + 12 + 1 values). A shared scalar is justified only if the per-layer means agree within the noise floor.
qa.decides: one scalar per norm per layer vs one scalar shared across layers

qa.q: Should the new scalars sit in a no-decay group?
qa.a: With decoupled decay, the equilibrium needs a normalized Adam step of wd·p ≈ 0.1–0.14 for p ≈ 1–1.4. A weak but persistent gradient bias therefore suffices, and decay pulls each scalar down by up to about 0.32 (to 0.681 of its value) when the gradient carries no signal. If the baseline means come out near 0.68, decay is what set them, so exempt the scalars. If the means are clearly above 1, gradient dominates and the choice barely matters.
qa.decides: leave them in AdamW "other" with wd 0.1 vs edit `build_optimizers` to add a wd = 0 group

nodes.focus: What is the paired A/A floor: the sd of the `mean(loss_curve[29:45])` difference between two same-seed baseline reruns?

qa.q: Is the A/A floor the right noise term for the kill check, or only a lower bound on it?
qa.a: It is only a lower bound. In A/A both runs compute the same function, so they differ only through floating-point nondeterminism. In A/B the arms differ from step 1, so the paired difference also carries seed×arm interaction: how differently the two arms react to the same init and batches. The sd that L4 needs (sd_d < 0.00124) is the across-seed sd of (B−A), which only the arm runs can measure. The A/A floor can only show that the threshold is impossible (if the floor is already above 0.00124). It cannot show that the threshold is met.
qa.decides: kill threshold from A/A reruns vs kill threshold from the across-seed sd of the arm differences (B−A)

qa.q: Do two same-seed baseline reruns produce bitwise-identical `loss_curve`s?
qa.a: Unknown until run, but nonzero is likely. Two parts of the run are possible sources: - **Attention.** q/k have head dim 64+32 = 96 and v has 64, which likely rules out the flash kernel and routes SDPA to the memory-efficient kernel. That kernel's backward uses atomic accumulation (belief; https://pytorch.org/docs/stable/notes/randomness.html). - **cuBLAS.** It is only guaranteed reproducible with `CUBLAS_WORKSPACE_CONFIG` set (https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cublas/index.html#results-reproducibility). One rerun pair compared with `loss_curve[0] == loss_curve[0]` and then elementwise settles it. S
qa.decides: floor = 0 (pairing exact, no A/A runs needed beyond one check) vs floor > 0 (measure it over several pairs)

qa.q: Which mode must the A/A runs use?
qa.a: Use `--smoke-seconds`, with S large enough to pass 45 steps. Pick S as 45 × (step time from the 3-step smoke) × 1.3. Under `--smoke-steps 45`, steps 30–45 are a cooldown that the full run never sees, so a floor measured there does not transfer. Both arms and the A/A pairs must use the same mode.
qa.decides: `--smoke-seconds S` (schedule identical to the full run) vs `--smoke-steps 45` (warm = 1, cooldown from step 31)

qa.q: How many A/A pairs give a usable estimate of the floor?
qa.a: A/A differences have known mean 0, so the sd estimate sqrt(mean d²) has df = n. - **n = 3:** the 95% CI on the sd is roughly [0.57, 3.7] × estimate (χ²₃ quantiles 0.216 and 9.35). - **n = 6:** the CI is about [0.64, 2.2] × estimate. Three pairs only resolve whether the floor is near 1e-4, near 1e-3 or near 1e-2. Pinning it against 0.00124 within a factor of 1.5 needs about 6 pairs.
qa.decides: 3 pairs (one per existing seed) vs 6 pairs

qa.q: Can the three existing baseline seeds substitute for the A/A measurement?
qa.a: No. They are different seeds, so they give the unpaired sd, which contains everything the A/A floor removes. The data part of that unpaired noise can be estimated: - `mean(loss_curve[29:45])` averages 16 × 32,768 = 524k tokens. - At a per-token loss sd of about 2.5–3 nats, data sampling alone contributes about 0.004 (belief). Same-seed pairing cancels this term exactly, because `Shards` replays the same windows. The existing curves still give that unpaired sd for free, and it is the denominator of the pairing-gain ratio.
qa.decides: reuse existing curves vs new reruns

qa.q: Does adding s and b, or a counted-unigram init, change the batches or the init of the other weights?
qa.a: - **Init.** Zero or constant init (`torch.zeros`, `torch.full`) consumes no torch RNG, so `self.apply(self._init)` draws the same normals for every existing weight. Any new `nn.Linear` would break that, because `_init` re-draws it. - **Batches.** A counted-unigram init that calls `train.sample` would advance `train.rng` and shift every batch. Counting must read a memmap slice directly (e.g. `np.bincount` on the first shard) and must not reuse `train.rng`. If either rule is broken, the pairing is gone and the A/B noise reverts to the unpaired sd.
qa.decides: create the new tensors with constants and count from a separate reader vs any construction that consumes RNG

qa.q: Does the divergence between reruns grow with step, so that the 30–45 window is noisier than steps 1–26?
qa.a: Unknown. Belief: the perturbation starts at bf16 rounding scale (about 1e-3 relative in some gradients) and grows chaotically. Steps 30–45 sit right after warmup ends at step 30, at peak Muon LR 0.02, which is the most divergence-amplifying stretch. The A/A curves give the floor per step for free: sd of d_t for each t, across pairs. Report it for steps 1–26 and 29:45 separately.
qa.decides: use the floor from 29:45 for L1's steps 1–26 too vs measure a separate floor per window

qa.q: Does the 4-decimal rounding in `loss_curve` matter at this floor?
qa.a: No. Rounding to 1e-4 gives a per-step error sd of about 2.9e-5; averaged over 16 steps that is about 7e-6. This is far below the 0.00124 threshold (script: `round(float(l), 4)`).
qa.decides: read losses from `loss_curve` vs add an unrounded log

qa.q: Should the A/A check run with `torch.use_deterministic_algorithms(True)` and a math-SDPA fallback, to drive the floor to 0?
qa.a: Deterministic mode would make A/A trivially 0, which is uninformative. It could also force a slower or more memory-hungry SDPA path, which C4 forbids in the shipped script. The floor must be measured with the production kernels, because those are what the arm runs use. Determinism would only help as a diagnostic, to show that the nondeterminism comes from SDPA rather than cuBLAS.
qa.decides: deterministic measurement build vs production kernels

qa.q: Does C7 acceptance benefit from pairing at all?
qa.a: No. C7 is a one-sided Welch test on exam val loss, which is unpaired by construction. Pairing only sharpens the 45-step kill check (L1, L4). For acceptance, L5's arithmetic stands: at an exam sd of about 0.004, a gain of about 0.017 or more is needed with 3+3 seeds.
qa.decides: invest in paired runs vs invest in more unpaired seeds for the exam

Scale-invariant weights trained with decay grow their norm through tangential steps until decay balances it (https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.08419). AdamW's per-coordinate normalisation also leaves a radial component, so L3's "norm set only by input and decay" is incomplete.

The head is `nn.Linear` with weight tied to `tok.weight`, applied to `self.norm(x.mean(dim=2))`. Logits stay bf16 under autocast and the loss is plain F.cross_entropy.
`param_counts` subtracts only `tok.weight`, so s and b (2 × 50304 = 100,608) count as non-embedding: 21.24M → about 21.34M, cap about 23.36M. A frozen buffer would not count.
`named_parameters` dedupes the tie, so only `tok.weight` appears; it goes to AdamW (lr 3e-3, wd 0.1, betas 0.9/0.95). New 1-D vectors fall to AdamW too, but need their own wd = 0 group.
Steps = 50e6 / 32768 = 1525; accum = 8 micro-batches of 4×1024; warmup 2%, cooldown 30%.
Initial row RMS is 0.02 and RMSNorm output RMS is 1. Initialise s = log(0.02) for RMS-normalised rows so step-0 logits match baseline.
Logits tensor per micro-batch is 4096×50304 bf16 ≈ 412 MB. Never add a logits-sized elementwise op; fold s into the weight and b into F.linear.
The exam builds GPT(cfg) and loads `state_dict`. The prior must be a Parameter or persistent buffer filled in main before training, never computed in `__init__`.
Mean over Sinkhorn-mixed streams preserves the input, so the readout always contains exactly e_x plus branch writes.
At step 100, the rank-10k+ band is 11.613 nats on 12% of tokens; the rank 0–100 band is 3.163 on 42%; step-26 loss is 7.06.
Layer-0 gradient is anomalously high (attn 0.24–0.29, about 10x layer 1) on 3 seeds. It is a possible readout of input-side pressure; watch it in both arms.
