nodes.focus: How far do the read logits on Muon actually move by step 100 and by the end?

qa.q: Does the size of the Muon update on `read_logits` depend on the size of its gradient at all?
qa.a: No. `newton_schulz5` divides by the Frobenius norm and then orthogonalises, so every step's update has singular values of roughly 0.5–1.5 (https://kellerjordan.github.io/posts/muon/), and `scale = max(1, 2/4)**0.5 = 1`. The step is about `lr·m·(1–1.4)` in Frobenius norm whether the gradient is 1e-2 or 1e-6. Only a gradient with norm near the `1e-7` eps gets damped.
qa.decides: L2 measured as logit movement vs L2 measured as a signal test such as update sign-consistency

qa.q: What is the lr-integrated movement budget at step 100 and at the end?
qa.a: The run is 1525 steps, warm=30, cool_start=1067. Σ multiplier is 15.5+70 = 85.5 by step 100, giving Σlr = 1.71. Over the whole run it is 15.5+1037+229.5 = 1282, giving Σlr = 25.6. At 45 steps Σlr is only about 0.65, so a 45-step sweep sees at most a third of the step-100 movement.
qa.decides: smoke length of 45 steps vs 100+ steps for any read-movement check

qa.q: What is the ceiling on read movement if the gradient direction were perfectly consistent?
qa.a: The softmax gradient has zero row sum, so each update row is orthogonal to 1. The most a unit row can put on one entry is √(3/4) = 0.87. The ceiling is therefore about 1.5 logit units on the favoured entry by step 100, which gives a weight of about 0.70, i.e. max |w−0.25| ≈ 0.45. Under weight decay the equilibrium is |p| ≈ 0.87/0.1 ≈ 8.7, and 1−e^(−0.1·25.6) = 92% of it is reached by the end, which means near one-hot reads.
qa.decides: bounded read (clamp or decay-only) vs free read

qa.q: Is the read gradient direction consistent (signal) or noise?
qa.a: Unknown. At init the gradient is proportional to `<x_j − x̄, G>`, and the stream differences come from 2% write asymmetry plus bf16 rounding, so noise is plausible. If it is noise, Muon still takes full-size steps, and momentum 0.95 (persistence ≈ 20 steps) makes this a correlated random walk. My estimate (belief) is about 0.2–0.4 per entry by step 100, i.e. |w−0.25| ≈ 0.04–0.08, and an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck std of about 0.9 per entry by the end, i.e. |w−0.25| ≈ 0.15–0.2.
qa.decides: keep reads on Muon vs move them to AdamW (Adam shrinks zero-mean gradients, Muon does not)

qa.q: Do `write_logits`, also 2-D on Muon, move just as fast and make the "2% asymmetry" an init-only fact?
qa.a: Yes, the same arithmetic applies. By step 100 the write logits can move by up to about ±1.5, so gains of 1.015/0.995 can become roughly 1.6/0.4. Even a noise walk of ±0.3 gives gains of about 1.15/0.85. Stream differences will be set by Muon's write drift within tens of steps, not by the init.
qa.decides: keep write logits on Muon vs freeze them or move them to AdamW to isolate the mixing effect

qa.q: Does read row 0 of block 0 (the attention read in the first block) receive any gradient?
qa.a: Its input streams are always identical copies of the embedding, so any convex read gives the same output and its gradient is zero up to rounding. Inside NS5 that row is just a near-zero row of the 2×4 matrix; it is amplified at most about 3.44⁵ ≈ 490× relative, which stays negligible. It is a dead parameter and should be excluded from the 24-stage max (23 live stages).
qa.decides: include vs exclude it from the L2 max; keep vs drop that parameter

qa.q: Is the stream state bf16, and does that hide small read changes?
qa.a: Belief: yes. The `einsum` in `combine` runs under autocast, its inner bmm returns bf16, and `weights.to(x.dtype)` then rounds read weights to bf16. Near 0.25 the bf16 spacing is about 0.001–0.002, so deviations below 0.002 are invisible in the forward pass. The same rounding also turns 2% stream differences into partly quantised noise.
qa.decides: measure read weights from the fp32 parameter vs from the forward; keep `combine` in bf16 vs force fp32

qa.q: Does Muon weight decay limit how far the reads and writes can go by the end?
qa.a: Yes. `p.mul_(1 − lr·0.1)` gives an e-fold time of 500 full-lr steps. A consistent direction saturates at about 8.7 per entry (Q3), and noise settles near ±0.9. Decay does not prevent near one-hot reads if the signal is consistent.
qa.decides: exclude stream gates from weight decay vs keep decay 0.1

qa.q: Does lowering the mix init change how far the reads move?
qa.a: Not in magnitude, since Muon fixes the step size. It can change direction consistency: more exchange makes the streams more alike, so `x_j − x̄` shrinks toward rounding noise. Low inits are therefore more likely to show large but random read movement. Unknown until measured.
qa.decides: one shared L2 gate vs a per-init L2 gate

qa.q: Can gradient clipping or the Muon eps stop read movement?
qa.a: Clipping rescales the gradient, but NS5 then normalises it again, so clipping has no effect on direction. Only a read-gradient norm below about 1e-7 after clipping would shrink the step. That seems unlikely but is unmeasured, so log `‖grad(read_logits)‖` per stage.
qa.decides: logging the read-gradient norm vs not

assumes: Read and write gates belong on Muon like weight matrices, not on AdamW.
Read weights are convex (softmax, sum to 1).
Logit movement means the mixing affects the loss, i.e. movement is signal, not optimiser-forced noise.
Write asymmetry stays near 2%, so stream spread starts small.
Stream differences survive bf16 storage.
A 45-step smoke is long enough to rank mixing inits.
Weight decay on the stream gates is harmless.
inherited: `mix_logits` is a (2,4,4) Parameter initialised to 6·I. At init the diagonal is 0.9926 and each off-diagonal is 0.00246, not 99.75% identity as the variant states.
Sinkhorn ends with a column normalisation, so column sums are exactly 1 in fp32 and the stream mean is invariant to M.
All 4 streams start as the same copy of the embedding (`unsqueeze(2).expand`). The read logits are zeros, so every read is the mean, and the output is `x.mean(dim=2)`.

Write gains are 2·sigmoid(logit), which is 1.015 on the favoured stream and 0.995 elsewhere. The streams therefore differ by only about 2% of each write. Stage 0 favours stream 0, stage 1 favours stream 1, and streams 2 and 3 are never favoured.
`read_logits` and `write_logits` are 2-D, so they go to Muon at lr 0.02 with weight decay 0.1. `mix_logits` is 3-D, so it goes to AdamW at 3e-3 with weight decay 0.1.
The effective learning-rate sum over the run is about 1281 steps × lr: 1525 steps, 30 warmup, 458 cooldown.
The change adds 0 parameters and costs no extra memory or step time; C3 and C4 are untouched.
Single-stream baseline at step 100: RMS growth ×7.8, loss 6.1789, layer-0 attention gradient 0.24 against about 0.02 elsewhere.
Static HC ×4 reaches an OLMo-1B eval loss of 2.791, against 2.781 for dynamic ×4. https://arxiv.org/pdf/2409.19606
On a 30M nanoGPT, alternative doubly-stochastic parameterisations reach only parity. https://arxiv.org/pdf/2604.02309

qa.q: Does the measured entropy profile support the premise that deep attention is near-uniform?
qa.a: No. Entropy is highest at layer 0 (0.957), then layers 1 (0.903) and 2 (0.854). Layers 10 and 11 are 0.711 and 0.763, ranked 8th and 7th. By the idea's own rule ("if the last two blocks are not the highest-entropy layers, drop the idea"), the 100-step data already says drop it. The rationale is inverted: extra attention would go into the *most* uniform layers. The layout may still be right for other reasons (sandwich ordering, below), so the gate should be a zero-ablation of deep attention on a trained baseline checkpoint, scored on train-shard windows, not entropy.
qa.decides: run the idea's own entropy gate vs replace it with an ablation gate

qa.q: Is there prior evidence for "more attention at the bottom, more FFN at the top" that does not depend on the entropy argument?
qa.a: Yes. Press, Smith and Levy's sandwich transformer put extra attention sublayers at the bottom and extra FFN sublayers at the top, with the same sublayer count. It improved WikiText-103 and enwik8 language modelling, but the gain did not transfer to translation (https://arxiv.org/abs/1911.03864; recalled, not fetched this session). PAR Transformer similarly kept quality with fewer attention layers, placed mostly early (https://arxiv.org/abs/2009.04534; recalled). The idea's +0.53M params is a confound, so a parameter-neutral reorder is the needed control.
qa.decides: keep the 13/12 non-neutral layout vs a parameter-neutral 12/12 reorder as the primary build

qa.q: In blocks 0–2, should the stage order be A-A-M or A-M-A?
qa.a: A-A-M follows the sandwich pattern and lets the second attention read the first one's output before any MLP. A-M-A interleaves, which gives A,M,A,A,M,A,A,M,A,A,M… and just shifts where the doubled attention falls. Build A-A-M; it is the faithful reading of "a second attention stage".
qa.decides: A-A-M vs A-M-A

qa.q: How should per-stage stream logits be shaped so the optimizer routing does not change silently?
qa.a: In the script, `read_logits` and `write_logits` have shape (2,4), so the `p.ndim == 2` rule sends them to **Muon**. `mix_logits` (2,4,4) is 3-D and goes to AdamW. If the builder splits them per stage into 1-D (4,) tensors, they silently move to AdamW at lr 3e-3. Keep shapes (S,4), (S,4,4) with S = number of stages in the block. Note that MLP-only blocks then have (1,4) rows, and Muon normalises them to a unit row; that is still Muon and acceptable, but it should be noted.
qa.decides: per-block (S,4) / (S,4,4) tensors vs per-stage 1-D parameters

qa.q: Is checkpointing block 0 needed?
qa.a: Probably not. Activations for one attention stage including the four-stream tensors (each (4,1024,4,384) bf16 = 12.6 MB) come to roughly 80–120 MB, and the net change is +1 stage, about +0.1 GB. Baseline peak is unmeasured here, but "micro_batch 8 spilled past 6 GB" suggests micro_batch 4 sits around 3–3.5 GB. Build without checkpointing, read peak_vram_gb from `--smoke-steps 20`, and add checkpointing only if peak goes above 5.3 GB. Checkpointing also recomputes the Sinkhorn loops and adds code surface under the tripwire.
qa.decides: torch.utils.checkpoint on block 0 vs no checkpointing

qa.q: Do the deep attention stages carry copying/recall work that MLP-only blocks cannot do?
qa.a: Unknown at 21M / 50M tokens. At large scale, deep attention layers are the most removable by input/output similarity (He et al., https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.15786; recalled). Here the recall gap is 2.23 nats and nothing shows which layers produce it. The zero-ablation of block 10 and block 11 attention, separately, on a trained baseline decides this.
qa.decides: drop attention in both blocks 10 and 11 vs only block 11

qa.q: Can the step-45 kill threshold (+0.03) be resolved?
qa.a: Total steps = 50e6 // 32768 = 1525, and warmup = 30 steps, so step 45 is just past warmup. Loss falls about 0.019 per step there (7.062 at step 26, 6.590 at step 51), so a one-step lag reads as +0.02. Per-batch noise is unmeasured. Use the mean loss over steps 40–50, averaged over the same seeds for both arms.
qa.decides: a single-seed step-45 comparison vs a 3-seed mean over steps 40–50

qa.q: Is a −0.01 gain detectable under C7 with 3 seeds?
qa.a: Likely not. With n=3 per arm (Welch df ≈ 4, one-sided t₀.₀₁ ≈ 3.75), beating the baseline by 0.005 plus a margin requires a seed std below about 0.0016 for a true effect of 0.01. Seed std at 50M tokens is unmeasured. Plan 5 seeds (t ≈ 2.9, which needs std below about 0.0027).
qa.decides: 3 seeds vs 5+ seeds per arm

qa.q: How will the exam reconstruct the layout?
qa.a: The exam calls GPT(cfg) built from the saved config. Whether it uses the candidate's Config class is unknown. Derive the layout in code (or read it with `getattr(cfg, "layout", DEFAULT)`) so an exam-side Config without the field still builds the same model. A string field with a default also works through the auto-generated argparse.
qa.decides: a new Config field vs a layout derived in code from n_layer

qa.q: What write-stream init should the third stage get?
qa.a: It barely matters. 2·sigmoid(0.03) = 1.015 vs 2·sigmoid(−0.01) = 0.995, and mixing starts near identity (off-diagonal about 0.0025 after Sinkhorn on exp(6) diagonals). The streams stay nearly identical early on. Use stream s mod 4 for consistency. nodes.focus: Are the measured baseline numbers from the MHA nano-GPT2 baseline or from this MLA script? Does the MLA script already trail the pooled baseline?

qa.q: Does the 21.24M baseline parameter count show which script the measurements came from?
qa.a: No. The two models are parameter-matched to within about 1k, so the count fits both. MHA at d_ff=1024 has 4×147,456 attention + 3×384×1024 MLP + 768 norms = 1,770,240 per block, 21,243,264 total. This MLA script at d_ff=1077 has 1,770,160 per block, 21,242,304 total. d_ff=1077 is evidently the parameter-matching choice: the 53 extra FFN columns (61,056) offset the MLA saving of 61,184.
qa.decides: treat the step-26/51/100 numbers as this MLA script's own baseline vs. re-measure them on this script before any comparison

qa.q: Can the loss baselines (7.0622 at step 26, 6.5902 at step 51, recall 4.475 at step 100) be compared with a 45-step smoke run?
qa.a: No. `--smoke-steps N` sets `total_steps = N`, and `lr_mult` scales with it. A 45-step run has warmup of 1 step and cooldown from step 31. The full run (1525 steps) has a 30-step warmup and no cooldown before step 1067. A step-100 number can only come from a run of at least 100 steps, so it used a different schedule from the 45-step test. The step-40-to-45 KILL needs a baseline run of this script with `--smoke-steps 45`, on the same seeds.
qa.decides: KILL measured against those numbers vs. KILL measured against a fresh baseline run with an identical `--smoke-steps 45`

qa.q: Which script produced the layer-0 gradient, attention-mass and recall/rare measurements?
qa.a: Unknown; I found no logs. The first-token mass needs explicit attention probabilities, since SDPA does not return them. In this script the probe would have to rebuild `cat(qc_norm, qr)·cat(k_norm, kr)` with the 96-dim scale; an MHA probe would not carry over. The layer-0 gradient spike could also come from the 4-stream embedding broadcast, which the MHA baseline does not have.
qa.decides: trust the layer-0 anomaly and the absence of a sink as properties of this MLA + 4-stream model vs. re-probe them

qa.q: Does this MLA + mHC script already trail the pooled baseline mean on the exam?
qa.a: Unknown. No exam loss for this script is given, and the pooled baseline mean is not given either. Published evidence at small scale is mixed: MLA without RoPE trailed MHA by 3–5% at 30M (https://arxiv.org/html/2506.09342v2). The decoupled-rotary variant used here is the one that avoided rank collapse (https://arxiv.org/html/2507.09394v1), but that paper gives no matched loss figure that I can cite.
qa.decides: aim the gate at beating the baseline by 0.005 vs. treat the gate first as recovering an MLA deficit (or drop MLA and gate an MHA key/value path)

qa.q: Is the C7 comparator the MHA nano-GPT2 pool or this script?
qa.a: The pool is the harness baseline, which the docstring names as nano-GPT2 MHA (nano_specs.md section A). Even so, this script's own 3-seed exam is needed to separate "the gate helps" from "MLA/mHC hurt". If the gate's gain is smaller than an existing MLA deficit, the candidate fails C7 even though the gate works.
qa.decides: 3 seeds of this script as a control arm vs. relying only on the harness pool

qa.q: Is L1's "gate CV above 0.1" test informative?
qa.a: No; it passes trivially at initialisation. The gate input is the normed read, so gate pre-activations have std ≈ 0.02·√384 ≈ 0.39. silu(z) for z ~ N(0, 0.39²) has mean ≈ 0.04 and std ≈ 0.2, which gives a CV of several units before any training. A useful check is the top-16 energy share against the ungated latent and against the gate's own value at step 0, or the gate's correlation with token identity.
qa.decides: keep the CV metric vs. replace it with a change-from-init or a per-token selectivity metric

qa.q: Does the gate threaten C4 (VRAM or step time)?
qa.a: It is unlikely to. At micro-batch 4 the extra activations are about 3 × 4·1024·128 × 2 bytes ≈ 3 MB per layer, about 38 MB over 12 layers. The extra matmul is 384×128 per token, about 2% of block FLOPs. The 3-step smoke is enough, but the step-time ratio must be measured against the baseline, not against this script.
qa.decides: run a full VRAM rung vs. a 3-step smoke being enough

qa.q: Does the product start near the old linear code, as L3 hopes?
qa.a: No. At std 0.02 the latent ≈ RMSNorm(compress(x) ⊙ (gate(x)/2 + gate(x)²/4)), a roughly bilinear code with random signs per channel. RMSNorm restores its scale, so the result is not the old linear image. If L3's early-loss check fails, an offset of about +2 on the gate pre-activation (silu ≈ linear-scaled, near-constant) is the fallback; with `bias=False` that needs an extra parameter of 128 values.
qa.decides: plain gate init vs. a gate bias or offset init (silu(g+c)) that starts the latent close to the linear code

nodes.cluster_name: Slow batch-level gain on MLP write
nodes.focus: What is the per-layer MLP write RMS vs attention write RMS in the baseline at steps 0, 45, 100 and 1525?

qa.q: What is the per-layer MLP write RMS vs attention write RMS at step 0?
qa.a: From the init (calculated, not measured): the MLP write is about 0.011 in every layer. RMSNorm input gives gate and up entries of std 0.02·√384 = 0.392, silu(g)·u has RMS about 0.081, and w_down contributes 0.00408·√1077 = 0.134. The attention write is 0.080·rms(y) with v std 0.226. Attention near 0.82-std logits over up to 1024 positions puts it between about 0.0015 and 0.018, most likely 0.002–0.005. So at init the MLP write is roughly 3–7x the attention write. Both are large relative to the 0.02-RMS embedding stream.
qa.decides: apply the gain control to MLP only vs to both sublayers

qa.q: What do the measured numbers bound for the combined write per block at step 100?
qa.a: By the triangle inequality, each block's combined write RMS is at least its residual increment: at least 1.3 early and at least 0.65 late. If writes were orthogonal to the stream, they would be about √(2.7²−1.4²) ≈ 2.3 early and √(10.9²−10.25²) ≈ 3.7 late. The split between MLP and attention is unknown. Either way, the writes are about 60–300x their init size by step 100.
qa.decides: initialise exp(a) at the init write level (about 0.011) vs at the expected trained level (about 0.3–2)

qa.q: How far can `a` move under the default AdamW group?
qa.a: Adam moves a parameter by at most about lr per step. The summed lr multiplier is about 85.5 by step 100 (warmup 30) and about 1281 over 1525 steps. So |Δa| is at most about 0.26 nats by step 100 (1.29x) and about 3.8 nats over the whole run (47x). Weight decay on `a` would also pull exp(a) toward 1 at 3e-4 nats per step, which matters if a ≈ −4.5 (exp(a) = 0.011).
qa.decides: `a` in the AdamW "other" group (lr 3e-3, wd 0.1) vs its own group with higher lr and no weight decay

qa.q: Once c divides by the batch RMS, what else can still set the MLP write magnitude?
qa.a: The batch-level divide cancels both the matrix norms and the n2.weight scale. What remains is exp(a) (at most 1.3x by step 100, per A3) and 2·sigmoid(write_logits), which is capped at 2x. So by step 100 the MLP write would be at most about 2.6x exp(a)'s starting value, unlike attention, which stays free.
qa.decides: let n2.weight and write_logits keep training vs freeze them, or treat exp(a) as the only gain

qa.q: Does the raw (pre-c) MLP output keep growing under the gain control?
qa.a: Very likely yes, though unmeasured. Muon's step size does not depend on the gradient scale, so multiplying by c does not slow W's norm growth. Scale-invariant weights grow in norm under gradient training (https://arxiv.org/abs/1803.01814). If the raw output grows about 100x while exp(a) moves 1.3x, then exp(a)/ema falls below 0.02 and the gain-bound KILL fires whether or not the loss is fine.
qa.decides: kill on the bound exp(a)/ema ∈ [0.02, 50] vs kill only on exp(a) and loss

qa.q: How fast does the raw write grow per step, and what does that require of the EMA?
qa.a: The rate r is unmeasured. A 100x rise over 100 steps gives r ≈ 0.046 per step. With τ = 100 steps (0.99 per step), the warmup overshoot e^{rτ} is about 100x. With τ ≈ 10 steps it is about 1.6x. `forward` runs 8 times per optimizer step, so momentum 0.99 per micro-batch means τ ≈ 12.5 steps.
qa.decides: EMA momentum 0.99 vs 0.9, and updating per micro-batch vs per optimizer step

qa.q: Does the exam's forward update the EMA buffer?
qa.a: Unknown. The harness calls GPT(cfg).forward(idx), and whether it calls .eval() or no_grad is not shown. The buffer must be persistent so model.pt carries it. Any update during the exam would adapt to val data and make the result depend on order, so the update should be gated on both conditions.
qa.decides: gate the update on `self.training` vs on `torch.is_grad_enabled()` (or both)

qa.q: How do MLP and attention write magnitudes scale with uniform weight-norm growth?
qa.a: The MLP write is about cubic in matrix scale: silu(g) ≈ g/2 for small g, so silu(g)·u·W_down scales as gate × up × down. The attention write is quadratic (expand × wo). q and k are normalized, so their norms only change how peaked attention is. Uniform norm growth therefore inflates MLP writes fastest, which supports targeting the MLP first.
qa.decides: one gain mechanism for both vs MLP-specific

qa.q: Is the per-stream write equal to the residual increment, or does the 4-stream mixing split it?
qa.a: At init, Sinkhorn on exp(6·I) gives diagonal 403.4/406.4 ≈ 0.993 and off-diagonal ≈ 0.0025. The write weights are 2·sigmoid(≈0) ≈ 1. So the four streams start nearly identical and each receives the full branch output. Measuring the EMA on the branch output, before `combine`, is enough unless the mixing de-diagonalises later (unknown).
qa.decides: EMA on the branch output vs on the per-stream weighted write

qa.q: What equilibrium weight norm do Muon and decoupled weight decay reach, and when?
qa.a: The decay time constant is 1/(lr·wd) = 500 steps. For uncorrelated updates, the Frobenius equilibrium is about ‖U‖_F·√(lr/2wd) (rotational equilibrium, https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.17212). For w_down that is about 6.2, or 0.0096 per entry vs 0.0041 at init. For w_gate and w_up (Muon scale 1.675) it is about 10.4, or 0.016 per entry vs 0.02 at init. Correlated updates, which the near-linear stream growth suggests, push norms above this. The real trajectory is unknown.
qa.decides: expect raw growth to stop by about step 500 (fixed exp(a) suffices) vs expect continued drift (needs a fast `a`)

qa.q: Is the measured max logit of 22.75 (layer 8, step 100) produced by the RMS-normed content part or by the unnormalised rotary part?
qa.a: By step 100 the content part cannot be the main source. The cumulative AdamW lr multiplier over steps 1–100 is about 15 + 70 = 85, so each gain element moved by at most about 85 × 3e-3 ≈ 0.26 (Adam's per-step move is roughly bounded by lr). That gives g ≤ ~1.26 and a perfectly aligned content logit ≤ 64·1.26²/√96 ≈ 10.4. Most of the 22.75 must come from qr·kr/√96. Those vectors come from wq and self.rotary with no norm, so their scale is set by Muon. The idea's "gains grew to 1.9" is therefore inferred, not observed. Scaling the whole q is the faithful build, but the builder must log the conte
qa.decides: apply exp(τ) to the whole q (content + rotary) vs only to qc

qa.q: Is AdamW decay actually binding on the gains?
qa.a: Pure decay over the run is a factor of exp(−3e-4 × ~1281 effective steps) ≈ 0.68. Adam moves each element by up to 3e-3 per step against a decay pull of 5.7e-4 at g = 1.9. The equilibrium needs a gradient signal-to-noise ratio of only m/√v = wd·g ≈ 0.19, so the decay binds only where that ratio is weak. Whether it does is unknown until the baseline model.pt gains are dumped.
qa.decides: ship the bundle (exp(γ) + τ) vs τ alone with linear gains

qa.q: Does the baseline already have any per-head content temperature?
qa.a: No. q_norm and k_norm are RMSNorm(64) applied on the last dim of (B,H,T,64), so the 64 gains are shared across all 6 heads. Each head's content logit scale is identical. Per-head τ is new expressiveness and may be the real active ingredient, more than the decay-proofing. Build per-head as specified, and treat "τ-only" as the main ablation.
qa.decides: τ per head (6 per layer) vs one τ per layer

qa.q: How should a per-head scale go into SDPA?
qa.a: The `scale` argument of `F.scaled_dot_product_attention` takes only a Python float. Pre-multiplying q keeps the fused flash/efficient kernel and costs one extra (4,6,1024,96) bf16 tensor (~4.7 MB per layer). Materialising 4×6×1024×1024 scores per layer would cost VRAM and step time against C4. Use the pre-multiply.
qa.decides: pre-multiply q by exp(τ_eff)[None,:,None,None] with the default scale vs materialise QKᵀ with a tensor scale

qa.q: Which soft clip keeps τ = 0 exactly at 1/√96?
qa.a: The sigmoid form maps τ = 0 to exactly 0, ranges over (−1, 2), and has slope 2/3 at 0, so τ learns about 2/3 as fast. A hard clamp has zero gradient outside the range, so a head can get stuck at the bound. A centred tanh does not give 0 at τ = 0. Use the sigmoid form. Weight decay on the raw τ then returns it to the unit scale, which is the intended fixed point.
qa.decides: τ_eff = 3·σ(τ − ln 2) − 1 vs hard clamp(τ, −1, 2)

qa.q: Does exp(γ) change more than the decay fixed point?
qa.a: Yes. Adam's update on γ is multiplicative, so the effective step on g is lr·g: about 1.9× faster at g = 1.9 and slower below 1. The decay pull at the same g also drops about 3× (wd·ln 1.9 = 0.064 vs wd·1.9 = 0.19). Any result therefore confounds "decay-proof" with "faster gain learning". A third arm is needed to attribute a win.
qa.decides: bundle γ-reparam and τ in one arm vs add a control arm with linear gains + τ

qa.q: Can the 45-step smoke test discriminate at all?
qa.a: With --smoke-steps 45 the schedule compresses: warmup 1 step, cooldown from step 31. Total multiplier is about 31 + 7 = 38, so γ and τ move ≤ ~0.11 and the temperature changes by ≤ ~8%. The 45-step check can catch breakage (the +0.02 kill) but cannot show the mechanism. L1–L3 need ≥300 steps with per-layer logit and entropy dumps.
qa.decides: 45-step kill check vs a 300-step matched loss_curve comparison

qa.q: How exactly is "gain norm within 1.15 of 1.0" measured?
qa.a: The L2 norm of the initial 64-vector is 8, so the criterion must mean RMS or mean. The quantity that multiplies the logit is Σ_d g_q,d·g_k,d·q̂_d·k̂_d, so mean(g_q⊙g_k) per layer is the right metric. A kill threshold of 1.15² ≈ 1.32 on the product is equivalent.
qa.decides: kill on RMS(g) per norm vs on mean(g_q⊙g_k) per layer

qa.q: Is an upper bound of 2 safe?
qa.a: Unknown. QK-norm is the current guard against logit blow-up. At 7.4×, content logits could reach about 7.4 × 6.5 ≈ 48, and the unbounded rotary part could exceed that. fp32 softmax inside the kernels will not overflow, but entropy collapse and loss spikes are possible. Keep 2 as the idea says, and log max τ_eff per layer and loss spikes.
qa.decides: τ_max = 2 (7.4× logits) vs τ_max = ln 3 (3×)

qa.q: Is there prior evidence at this scale?
qa.a: QKNorm with a learnable g gave +0.928 BLEU on small MT models (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2010.04245). SSMax reports faster pretraining loss reduction (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2501.19399). Unclipped learned per-token temperature drifted and hurt performance (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2310.12956). I know of no sub-100M LM ablation with MLA and decoupled RoPE. Clipping is supported by that evidence; the size of the effect is unknown.
qa.decides: prioritise this over the other OPEN temperature variants vs not

qa.q: Is the predicted 0.02–0.04 nats arithmetically reachable through recall tokens alone?
qa.a: Recall tokens are 13% of targets (measured). A 0.02 net gain needs about 0.15 nats on them, and 0.04 needs about 0.31 nats, assuming zero cost elsewhere. That is a large recall gain, so the build cannot also afford a 0.01 loss on the other 87% of targets. This argues for logging both groups from the first run.
qa.decides: 3 shifted heads per layer vs 1 shifted head per layer (lower cost to L4)

qa.q: How should the shifted key at position 0, which has no predecessor, be filled?
qa.a: `torch.roll` wraps token T−1's key into position 0. That puts future content into a key every query can see, so it is a leak and must not be used. The safe choice is a zero key: `cat([zeros_like(k[:,:,:1]), k[:,:,:-1]], dim=2)`. It gives logit 0, so query 0 attends only to j=0 and reads its own value (no NaN). Watch whether position 0 becomes a sink for heads 3–5; baseline first-token mass is 0.002–0.006.
qa.decides: a zero key vs `torch.roll` (or a duplicate of token 0's key)

qa.q: Should the whole key be shifted (content plus rotary, post-RoPE), or only the content slice with rotary at j?
qa.a: The idea specifies post-RoPE, so shift the whole key. The rotary score then sees relative offset i−j+1, and purely positional heads still work, offset by one. `kr` is a single head expanded to all heads, so the simplest faithful build shifts the final `k` tensor for heads 3:6 after the `torch.cat`. Both variants are causal.
qa.decides: shift the final concatenated `k[:, 3:6]` vs shift `self.k_norm(k)` only and keep `kr` at j

qa.q: Can QK-norm logits get sharp enough to pick one matching token out of ~1000?
qa.a: With norm weights at 1, the content logit is at most 8·8/√96 ≈ 6.5 (SDPA scale is 1/√96 because q has 96 dims). Selecting one position among ~1000 needs a gap of about ln(1000) ≈ 6.9. The baseline already grows its max logit to 7.8–22.75 by step 100 (measured), so the norm gains learn this quickly. Keep init 1 for fidelity.
qa.decides: keep the `q_norm`/`k_norm` weight init at 1 vs raise it (e.g. 2)

qa.q: Does induction even form inside 50M tokens (1525 steps), and when?
qa.a: Unknown for this recipe. Olsson et al. report the induction phase change in small models at roughly 2.5–5B tokens with large batches (https://transformer-circuits.pub/2022/in-context-learning-and-induction-heads/index.html). This setup has a different optimizer, batch and LR, so that does not transfer. At step 45 (1.47M tokens) neither model likely has induction, so the 45-step kill tests only harm, not benefit.
qa.decides: trust the 45-step kill vs add a matched 300-step run before the 3-seed run

qa.q: Which layers should get shifted heads?
qa.a: Unknown. The mechanism needs the key to reflect token j−1's identity, which is cleanest in early layers where the residual is close to the embedding. Later layers already mix in neighbour information through standard heads. Build it as specified, but log the L1 attention share per layer so a specialised version can be chosen from data.
qa.decides: heads 3–5 in all 12 layers (as specified) vs only in layers 0–5

qa.q: Does it fit C3 and C4?
qa.a: It adds no parameters, so non-embedding stays at 21.24M. Each layer holds an extra (4,3,1024,96) bf16 tensor, about 2.4 MB, roughly 28 MB across 12 layers; that is negligible against 5.6 GB. SDPA keeps `is_causal=True`, so the fused kernel path is unchanged. A `cat` of a slice should stay within ~1% step time, but measure it in the 3-step timing check.
qa.decides: `cat`-based shift inside `Attention.forward` vs a precomputed index gather

qa.q: Can the exam harness rebuild the shifted model from `model.pt`?
qa.a: Unknown how `nano/exam.py` maps the saved config onto `Config`. Hardcoding (heads `n_head//2:` shifted) reproduces the model whatever the harness does with extra keys. A field with a default equal to the new behaviour is also safe if the exam instantiates this file's `Config`.
qa.decides: hardcode the shift vs add a Config field (e.g. `shift_heads: int = 3`)

qa.q: Does the layer-0 gradient anomaly (10× attention grad) interact with the shift?
qa.a: Unknown. Layer 0 is where one-hop induction is most natural, which is an argument for keeping it. Log layer-0 attention grad norm (baseline 0.2406 at step 100) and see whether it moves.
qa.decides: shift in layer 0 vs start shifting at layer 1

nodes.focus: Is the read update direction consistent across steps (cosine of successive Muon updates above 0.5) or a noise walk?

qa.q: Can "cosine of successive Muon updates above 0.5" tell drift from noise at all, given momentum 0.95 with Nesterov?
qa.a: No. For pure i.i.d. gradient noise, the Nesterov update u_t = 1.95·g_t + 0.9025·buf_{t−1} has a lag-1 autocorrelation of 9.70/12.16 ≈ 0.80. Pure noise therefore passes the 0.5 threshold easily, and the criterion cannot refute anything. NS5 rescales singular values but keeps the momentum-induced overlap in direction, so the post-NS cosine stays high. This is arithmetic; the post-NS value is a belief.
qa.decides: use successive-update cosine as the L2 diagnostic vs use a momentum-free statistic (raw-gradient or half-batch cosine)

qa.q: Which statistic does separate signal from noise, and what null value does it have?
qa.a: Consecutive steps draw independent random windows, so the cosine of consecutive raw gradients (before momentum) has a null near 0 and a mean of about SNR²/(1+SNR²) under signal. The half-batch cosine (4 vs 4 micro-batches at the same step) estimates the same SNR without any parameter drift between the two samples, so it is the cleaner choice. Both need a diagnostic copy of the script; the candidate must not carry the hook. The actual SNR of the read gradient is unknown.
qa.decides: log consecutive raw `p.grad` cosines vs split each step's 8 micro-batches into two halves and log the cosine between the half-gradients

qa.q: How large is the read-logit excursion that a pure noise walk produces under Muon with weight decay 0.1? It sets the null for L2.
qa.a: Belief, by arithmetic. The per-row Muon step is about lr·1, since NS5 singular values are about 0.5–1.5 and the shape scale is 1 for 2×4 (https://kellerjordan.github.io/posts/muon/). The decay rate is γ = lr·0.1, and the integrated autocorrelation of the momentum update is about 33 steps. The stationary noise-walk norm is then about √(0.02²·33/(2·0.002)) ≈ 1.8 logits per row, reached within about 1/γ = 500 steps. That gives max |softmax − 0.25| of about 0.15–0.25 over 22 live rows, so L2's "> 0.05" passes with no signal. A consistent drift would instead reach about ‖u‖/wd ≈ 10 logits, which is
qa.decides: keep the L2 threshold at 0.05 vs replace it with a noise-null threshold or a displacement-efficiency test

qa.q: Does NS5 on the 2×4 gradient give a weak-signal row a full-size step?
qa.a: Yes, unless the two rows are nearly parallel. NS5 amplifies a small normalised singular value by about 3.4445⁵ ≈ 485, so any second singular value above roughly 1.5e-3 of ‖G‖_F ends near 0.7–1.2. The row with the weaker gradient (attention-read vs MLP-read) therefore takes a step as large as the dominant row's, whatever its SNR. Block 0 row 0 is the exception: its gradient is exactly zero, because four identical streams and a softmax backward give w·(g − Σwg) = 0. NS5 maps a zero row to a zero row, so that row stays put.
qa.decides: keep read_logits and write_logits as one 2×4 Muon matrix vs move them to AdamW or orthogonalise per row

qa.q: Over what window does a displacement test discriminate, and how expensive is it?
qa.a: By step 100 (Σlr = 1.71) a noise walk moves a row about √(100·0.0171²·33) ≈ 1.0 against a drift bound of 1.71. That is a ratio of about 0.57 vs 1.0, too close to call per row. Over a 400-step plateau window (path length 8), noise gives a net displacement of about 2.3 vs about 8 for drift, an efficiency of about 0.29 vs 1.0, which separates cleanly. A 45-step smoke cannot settle it; the half-batch cosine from A2 can, within about 50 steps, if SNR is not tiny. All figures are belief.
qa.decides: settle the question in a 45–100-step smoke vs a run of at least 400 steps

qa.q: Does the mix-logit init change the read-update direction or only its consequences?
qa.a: Muon's step size is independent of gradient magnitude (https://kellerjordan.github.io/posts/muon/), so lowering the mix init does not change how far the reads walk. It changes only the read SNR, through the stream spread, and that dependence is unknown. If reads are noise-dominated at every init, the sweep compares four noise walks, and L5's parity prior is the expected outcome whatever the mixing does.
qa.decides: sweep the mix init with read and write logits on Muon as now vs fix the read/write optimiser first and sweep the mix init second

qa.q: Is the stream spread that the reads see set by the 2% write init or by Muon noise on write_logits?
qa.a: Write logits share Q3's dynamics, so a noise walk with per-coordinate std of about 1 logit takes the gains 2σ(l) to roughly 0.5–1.5 across streams. That makes the 2% init asymmetry irrelevant after a few hundred steps. This is a belief and is unmeasured. It means the spread in L3 is mostly driven by write noise, and the reads are learning against a moving, noise-generated target.
qa.decides: interpret L3 as an exchange-vs-init effect vs an exchange-vs-write-noise effect (log write-gain spread alongside the stream spread)

qa.q: Does gradient clipping distort the read-direction measurement?
qa.a: No. `clip_grad_norm_` rescales all gradients by one scalar, so cosines are identical before and after clipping, and Muon's NS5 removes the scale anyway. Either point works; log after `backward` and before `o.step()`. The clip does change the magnitude of the AdamW-driven `mix_logits` updates, but not their direction.
qa.decides: log cosines on pre-clip `p.grad` vs on post-clip `p.grad`

qa.q: Does the Nesterov momentum buffer's own direction carry signal that the raw-gradient test would miss?
qa.a: The buffer averages about 20 gradients, so cos(buf_t, g'_t), with g'_t from an independent half batch, is about √(20)·SNR times larger than a single-gradient cosine at small SNR. It is a more sensitive test with the same null of 0. This is a belief. It costs one extra read of the optimiser state per logged step.
qa.decides: compare successive `st["buf"]` vs compare `buf` against an independent fresh half-batch gradient

nodes.cluster_name: Gated nonlinear KV path (latent or expansion)
nodes.focus: Exam val loss of this MLA script over 3 seeds against the pooled baseline mean

qa.q: Is the pooled baseline mean, and its seed count, available anywhere the builder can read?
qa.a: Unknown. No results file exists in either workspace. Without the mean and its n, nobody can say whether the gate has to close an MLA/mHC deficit before it can count under C7.
qa.decides: test the gate against the pooled MHA baseline vs a paired A/B of gate against this MLA+mHC script

qa.q: How many seeds does C7 actually need for a 0.01-nat effect?
qa.a: This is Welch arithmetic. If the pooled baseline has many seeds, the candidate's 3 seeds dominate: df ≈ 2, one-sided t₀.₉₉ = 6.965, SE ≈ 0.577σ, so the difference must exceed about 4.0σ. A 0.01 gain then passes only if the seed std σ ≤ 0.0025. With 3 against 3 (df ≈ 4, t = 3.747), the threshold is 3.06σ, so σ ≤ 0.0033. The seed std at 50M tokens is unknown. If it is 0.005 or more, 3 seeds cannot confirm a 0.01 gain.
qa.decides: 3 seeds per arm vs 5–6 seeds per arm

qa.q: How big a deficit does this script carry against MHA before the gate is added?
qa.a: Unknown for this exact configuration. MLA without RoPE trailed MHA by 3–5% at 30M parameters (https://arxiv.org/html/2506.09342v2). At a loss near 3.4 nats that is about 0.1–0.17 nats, ten times the predicted gate gain. The decoupled rotary path here should shrink the gap, but by an unmeasured amount.
qa.decides: run a 3-seed control of the ungated MLA script first vs go straight to the gate

qa.q: Does the residual stream stay in fp32 as it would in a single-stream baseline?
qa.a: Probably not (belief, unchecked). `tok(idx)` is fp32, but `torch.einsum` under autocast dispatches to `bmm` and returns bf16. From block 0 onward all 4 streams then accumulate in bf16. In a plain `x = x + branch` baseline, fp32 + bf16 promotes to fp32. This is a possible hidden deficit, and the builder can check it with one `print(x.dtype)` after block 0.
qa.decides: keep the einsum as written vs force `combine` to float32

qa.q: Which optimizer actually updates the mHC parameters?
qa.a: Read from the script: `read_logits` and `write_logits` have shape (2, 4), so `ndim == 2` sends them to Muon at lr 0.02. Muon orthogonalizes each 2×4 update, which couples the attention row and the MLP row and gives near-fixed-size steps whatever the gradient. `mix_logits` (2, 4, 4) is 3-D and goes to AdamW with weight decay 0.1. Whether this hurts is unknown. Changing it alters the substrate, so it must happen on both arms of any A/B.
qa.decides: leave the routing alone vs exclude `read_logits`/`write_logits` from Muon by name

qa.q: At init, is the gated latent still close to the old linear code?
qa.a: No. The gate pre-activation std is 0.02·√384 ≈ 0.39. That gives silu a mean of about 0.038 and a fluctuation std of about 0.2. The constant (linear-code) share of latent energy is therefore about 0.038²/(0.038² + 0.2²) ≈ 3.5%, so the step-0 latent is about 96% bilinear, and `latent_norm` hides the ×0.2 scale drop. This makes the L3 early-loss risk concrete. Zero-init plus silu is not an option: silu(0) = 0 gives a zero latent, and RMSNorm with eps 1e-6 then gives about 1000× gradient blow-up.
qa.decides: `silu(gate(x))` at std 0.02 vs `2*sigmoid(gate(x))` with a zero-init gate, which is exactly the linear code at step 0

qa.q: Does C4 hold for the ungated script, before the gate's extra 128-wide activation is added?
qa.a: Unknown, nothing measured. Two beliefs: the streams add about 4×384 bf16 values per token per stored tensor, roughly 12.6 MB per tensor per micro-batch, across several tensors per stage and 24 stages. Each forward also runs 2 × 20 Sinkhorn iterations × 12 blocks, about 1000 tiny kernels, 8 times per step, plus their backward. The baseline's `micro_batch=4` comment says 8 already spilled past 6 GB, so headroom is tight.
qa.decides: keep the 4-stream mHC substrate vs collapse it to one stream for this test

qa.q: Can early-step comparisons be matched to the full-run schedule?
qa.a: Yes, by the script. `--smoke-steps` overrides `total_steps`: warmup 1, cooldown from step 31 at N = 45, which is the compressed schedule. `--smoke-seconds` keeps `total_steps = 1525`: warmup 30, constant LR until step 1067. Its `loss_curve` is therefore step-for-step comparable to a full run and to the baseline's step-26/51/100 numbers, if those came from the full schedule.
qa.decides: judge the KILL on a 45-step `--smoke-steps` run vs the first N steps of `--smoke-seconds` runs

qa.q: Will the exam reload the gated model correctly?
qa.a: Either works if the exam builds `GPT(cfg)` from this file. A new `Config` field with a default survives `Config(**saved_config)`. A hardcoded `self.gate` is simply part of the `state_dict`. Whether the exam uses this file's classes, or what dtype it evaluates in, is unknown; `nano/exam.py` was not found.
qa.decides: hardcode the gate in `Attention` vs make it a `Config` flag

qa.q: Does the per-seed data order add variance on top of init variance?
qa.a: Yes, by the script. `Shards("train", ..., cfg.seed)` seeds the sampler, so seed k gives the same data order on both arms. A paired per-seed difference has lower variance than Welch's unpaired test, but C7 specifies Welch. The paired view is a diagnostic only.
qa.decides: compare arms with the same seed (paired) vs unpaired Welch only

nodes.cluster_name: Slow batch-level gain on MLP write
nodes.focus: Measured MLP and attention write RMS per layer at steps 45, 100, 1525

qa.q: What are the per-layer MLP and attention branch RMS values (output of `w_down` and `wo`, before `combine`) at steps 45, 100 and 1525 of the full 1525-step schedule?
qa.a: Unknown; nobody has measured them. Step-0 MLP output is ≈0.011 by calculation: gate and up pre-activations have std 0.02·√384 = 0.39, silu(g)·u has RMS ≈0.081, and w_down's gain is 0.00408·√1077 = 0.134. The residual increments of ≥1.3 per block at step 100 mean the combined writes have grown at least ~100x by then. An exp(a) initialised at the step-0 level would therefore pin the MLP about 100x below the baseline's.
qa.decides: initialise exp(a) at the step-0 level (≈0.011) vs at the measured trained level

qa.q: What share of each block's residual increment at step 100 comes from the MLP rather than attention?
qa.a: Unknown. At step 0 the attention write is position-dependent, roughly 0.018/√n_eff (v RMS 0.226 times wo gain 0.08, averaged over n_eff weakly-correlated positions). So the MLP dominates at step 0 everywhere except the first few positions. Nothing is known at step 100. If attention carries more than about half the increment, L2 cannot reach x3–x6.
qa.decides: gain on the MLP only vs gain on both branches

qa.q: Between step 100 and 1525, do MLP writes keep growing, plateau, or shrink?
qa.a: Unknown from measurement. Reasoning (belief) gives two bounds for decoupled weight decay with a 500-step time constant: - If Muon updates are uncorrelated across steps, the w_gate equilibrium Frobenius norm is √(η·s²·‖O‖²/2λ) ≈ 10.4. That is below its init norm of 12.9, so it would shrink. - If updates are fully aligned, ‖O‖/λ is far above init. Writes could therefore peak around step 100–500 and then fall through cooldown. A gain that tracks a learned constant would then fight the decay rather than the growth.
qa.decides: a slow EMA that runs all training vs a calibrate-then-freeze gain

qa.q: Can `a` reach the needed level in time if it stays in the AdamW "other" group?
qa.a: No. Summed lr to step 100 is 85.5 × 3e-3 ≈ 0.26 nats of maximum travel in log-gain. Tracking ~100x growth needs ≈4.6 nats. Weight decay on `a` also pulls exp(a) toward 1.0 RMS, an arbitrary target. `a` needs its own group with no weight decay, or a measured initial value.
qa.decides: `a` in the default AdamW group (lr 3e-3, wd 0.1) vs its own group (larger lr, no wd)

qa.q: Is the batch-level write RMS dominated by a few tokens (first position, delimiters) carrying massive activations?
qa.a: Unknown for this model. Massive activations concentrated in a few dimensions and tokens, produced by MLPs in middle layers, are documented in LLMs (https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.17762). If they appear here, a batch-RMS gain would scale down every ordinary token to cancel a handful of outliers.
qa.decides: plain mean-square EMA vs a robust statistic (clipped or median-of-token RMS)

qa.q: Does "step 45" mean `--smoke-steps 45` or step 45 of a full run?
qa.a: They differ. `--smoke-steps 45` sets total_steps = 45, so warmup is 1 step and cooldown starts at step 31. Summed lr multiplier ≈ 38.5 with lr falling at the end. In the full schedule, step 45 sits after a 30-step warmup at full lr, with summed multiplier ≈ 30.5. The KILL baseline (6.6–6.7 at steps 40–45) must come from the same mode as the candidate.
qa.decides: measure with `--smoke-steps 45` vs truncate a full-schedule run at step 45

qa.q: Should write RMS be measured on the branch output or on what actually lands in each stream?
qa.a: The stream increment is branch × 2σ(write_logits[stage, i]), plus Sinkhorn mixing of the old streams. At init the write weights are 1.015/0.995 and mixing is ≈0.993-diagonal, so the two are equal at step 0. Their later divergence is unmeasured. Log both: the branch RMS, and the branch RMS times the mean write weight.
qa.decides: place the gain before `combine` (branch) vs fold it into `write_logits` (per-stream)

qa.q: Will the EMA update during the harness exam?
qa.a: An ungated update in `forward` would change the buffer while the exam runs over validation windows. That makes exam outputs order-dependent and adapts a statistic on validation data. Whether `nano/exam.py` calls `model.eval()` is unknown, so the gate must be `self.training`, and the EMA must be frozen in eval. It updates 8 times per optimizer step (once per micro-batch), so τ in micro-batches = 8·τ in steps.
qa.decides: update the EMA inside `forward` gated by `self.training` vs update it from a hook called in the optimizer step

qa.q: How should the probe be taken without breaking C5/C6?
qa.a: Probe inside training. Steps 45 and 100 have no saved checkpoint, and the CLI must not change. - Draw one fixed probe batch once from `Shards("train", 1024, seed+12345)`. It must come from train only. - Read forward hooks on `b.mlp` and `b.attn` under `torch.no_grad()` in fp32. - Bin attention by position (<16, 16–256, 256–1024). - Write the results under a `probe` key in metrics.json at steps 1, 45, 100, 500, 1067 and the last step. The cost is three extra forward passes.
qa.decides: probe code inside the candidate script vs a separate diagnostic script loading checkpoints

known_tagged.text: Plug point is `MLP.forward` after `w_down`, before `Block.combine`; combine then scales per stream by 2·sigmoid(write_logits), range 0–2
Step-0 attention branch RMS ≈ 0.018/√n_eff, so it is largest at position 0 and small late in the sequence
Residual increments ≥1.3 per block early at step 100 imply ≥~100x write growth over init by step 100 [measured + belief]

By step 100, `n2.weight` can change by at most ≈±0.26 (AdamW, summed lr 85.5 × 3e-3), and write_logits by at most 2x. Early growth must therefore come from the matrices, so BREAKS holds early and is only partly true late [script + belief]
Muon's per-entry update per step at peak lr is ≈0.00061 for w_down (init entry 0.00408) and ≈0.00102 for w_gate/w_up (init 0.02)
Muon's decay uses the group lr without the shape scale; time constant 1/(lr·wd) = 500 steps (https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.17212)
Under uncorrelated updates, w_gate's equilibrium Frobenius norm (≈10.4) is below its init norm (12.9)
`--smoke-steps 45` compresses the schedule: warmup 1 step, cooldown from step 31
Full schedule summed lr multiplier to step 45 is 30.5
The EMA buffer must be persistent, updated only when `self.training`, and computed in fp32
Massive activations concentrate in a few tokens and dimensions and come from MLPs (https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.17762)
The probe batch must come from the train shards; val.bin must not appear anywhere (C6)
